options.A: Ask Claude to add requirements that store managers probably forgot, so that the list is as complete as possible from the start.
options.B: Ask Claude to summarise the notes in one paragraph.
options.C: Ask Claude to write the full new process design straight away from the notes, so stakeholders have something concrete to react to.
options.D: Ask Claude to extract distinct needs, group them by theme, mark must-have or nice-to-have with a quote, and list open questions.

questions.explanation: Claude is effective at structuring qualitative input into candidate requirements. Asking for themes, priorities, source quotes and open questions keeps the analysis traceable and highlights where stakeholders still need to decide.

why_incorrect.A: Invented requirements are not grounded in stakeholder input and should be raised as questions, not asserted.
why_incorrect.B: A single paragraph loses the individual needs, priorities and evidence that requirements work depends on.
why_incorrect.C: Designing before requirements are agreed skips the analysis and hides gaps in the notes.

questions.scenario: Lucerne Clinics' operations director lists ten ideas for using Claude and asks Mateo, an analyst, to recommend which to pilot first.
questions.question: Which TWO criteria should carry the most weight when using Claude to evaluate the use cases?

options.A: Which ideas use the largest number of Claude features at once, since broad pilots reveal more about the tool's capabilities.
options.B: Which ideas would remove the most staff roles.
options.C: The value of the outcome (time saved or quality gained) relative to the effort to set up the use case.
options.D: Which ideas would make the most impressive demonstration for the board, since visible early wins build support for wider adoption.
options.E: The risk if Claude's output is wrong, and whether a practical human review step exists.

questions.explanation: Good first pilots combine clear value, reasonable effort and manageable risk with a workable review step. Claude can help score options against these criteria, but the criteria themselves should reflect business outcomes and risk.

why_incorrect.A: Feature count is not a measure of value; simpler use cases often deliver more.
why_incorrect.B: Use-case selection should focus on value and risk; framing pilots around headcount cuts also tends to undermine adoption and trust.
why_incorrect.D: Demo appeal does not reflect sustained value or manageable risk.

questions.scenario: Claude helped Alpine Ski House draft user stories for a new rental booking process. In review, the finance team says none of the stories cover deposits and refunds, which are critical for them.
questions.question: What most likely went wrong in the requirements analysis?

options.A: The stories were written too briefly, so details such as deposits and refunds were cut out to save space.
options.B: The inputs did not include finance stakeholders' needs, so the stories could only reflect the views provided.
options.C: The model used was optimised for speed, so it skipped the less common parts of the booking process.
options.D: Claude avoids writing user stories that involve money, so financial requirements must always be written by hand.

questions.explanation: Requirements generated with Claude are only as complete as the stakeholder input supplied. Before drafting, list the stakeholder groups and confirm each group's needs are represented, or ask Claude to identify perspectives that seem to be missing.

why_incorrect.A: Length does not explain a whole missing stakeholder perspective.
why_incorrect.C: Missing coverage is caused by missing inputs, not by model speed.
why_incorrect.D: Claude can write financial user stories; it simply was not given that stakeholder input.

questions.scenario: Datum Corp's legal operations team wants to "use Claude for contract review." Requirements discussions keep stalling because people mean different things by the phrase.
questions.question: What is the most productive way to use Claude to move the analysis forward?

options.A: Ask Claude to break "contract review" into concrete use cases (clause extraction, playbook deviation flags, business summaries) with inputs, outputs and review points.
options.B: Ask Claude for a definition of contract review from a dictionary.
options.C: Postpone the analysis until a vendor can provide a ready-made solution.
options.D: Choose the broadest interpretation and ask Claude to design an end-to-end automated review of every contract, so nothing is left out.

questions.explanation: Vague requests become workable once they are decomposed into concrete use cases with defined inputs, outputs and human checkpoints. Claude is useful for producing that breakdown so stakeholders can compare and choose.

why_incorrect.B: A dictionary definition does not resolve which specific tasks the team needs.
why_incorrect.C: Delay does not clarify requirements; the team still needs to define what it wants.
why_incorrect.D: An undefined, all-encompassing scope increases risk and makes success hard to measure.

questions.scenario: A business analyst at Margie's Travel asks how Claude can best support requirements work without replacing stakeholder conversations.
questions.question: Which description is most accurate?

options.A: Claude replaces the need for a business analyst.
options.B: Claude should be used only after requirements are fully signed off, to turn them into polished documentation.
options.C: Claude can organise notes, draft requirements and suggest gaps, while stakeholders confirm priorities and decide.
options.D: Claude can determine the real business requirements from general industry knowledge, so stakeholder interviews become optional.

questions.explanation: Claude augments requirements analysis by structuring information and surfacing gaps. Ownership of priorities and decisions stays with the people accountable for the outcome.

why_incorrect.A: Claude augments the analyst's work; judgement, facilitation and decisions stay with people.
why_incorrect.B: Claude is helpful during analysis, for example structuring interview notes and spotting gaps.
why_incorrect.D: Claude cannot know an organisation's needs unless they are provided; stakeholders remain the source.

questions.scenario: Coho Winery's logistics coordinator wants to reduce the time it takes to process distributor orders. She can describe each step of the current process in detail.
questions.question: How can Claude help most effectively at the start?

options.A: Ask Claude to design a completely new order process from best practice, without describing the current one, to avoid bias.
options.B: Ask Claude to recommend new logistics software straight away, since a better tool is the fastest way to cut processing time.
options.C: Ask Claude to guarantee a 50% time reduction.
options.D: Ask Claude to map the steps, find hand-offs, delays and duplication, and suggest options to test, stating assumptions.

questions.explanation: Process optimisation starts with an accurate picture of the current state. Claude can map steps, highlight likely bottlenecks and propose experiments, as long as assumptions are explicit and results are tested in practice.

why_incorrect.A: Without the current process, Claude cannot identify where time is actually lost.
why_incorrect.B: Choosing tools comes after understanding where the bottlenecks are.
why_incorrect.C: Claude cannot guarantee outcomes for a process it has only seen described; results need testing.

questions.scenario: Graphic Design Institute's head of operations is planning a move to a new student information system next year and wants Claude to help build the project plan.
questions.question: Which TWO uses of Claude are most appropriate?

options.A: Drafting a phased plan with milestones, dependencies and risks based on the scope, dates and constraints she provides.
options.B: Producing a plan based only on a generic template with no institute details.
options.C: Committing the institute to final go-live dates based on Claude's draft, so the vendor can begin scheduling work straight away.
options.D: Approving the project budget on finance's behalf once Claude has estimated the costs from the vendor's price list.
options.E: Generating a checklist of questions to ask the vendor and internal teams to uncover hidden dependencies.

questions.explanation: Claude is a strong planning partner: it drafts structured plans from provided context and surfaces questions that reveal risks. Commitments and approvals remain with the accountable people.

why_incorrect.B: A generic plan ignores the institute's own constraints, systems and calendar.
why_incorrect.C: Plans need validation by the people doing the work; Claude's draft dates are a starting point, not commitments.
why_incorrect.D: Budget approval is a human governance decision, not something to delegate to Claude.

questions.scenario: Woodgrove Bank's procurement team wants a comparison of three document e-signature vendors' published security certifications and pricing models, using information from the vendors' public websites.
questions.question: Which approach best combines Claude's capabilities with verification?

options.A: Ask Claude in an ordinary chat to list each vendor's certifications and pricing from what it already knows, to save time.
options.B: Use research to gather and cite the vendors' published information, then confirm key claims with the vendors.
options.C: Accept the vendors' marketing claims without checking anything.
options.D: Ask Claude to compare the vendors and choose one, so the procurement team only needs to process the paperwork.

questions.explanation: Research tasks about third parties benefit from cited, current sources followed by targeted human confirmation, especially for claims that drive contractual or security decisions.

why_incorrect.A: Certifications change and recall may be outdated; current, cited sources are needed.
why_incorrect.C: Procurement decisions need claims confirmed, ideally with formal evidence.
why_incorrect.D: The decision and its accountability stay with the procurement team.

questions.scenario: Acme Logistics' planning team uses Claude to draft weekly driver schedules. A manager suggests asking Claude for the "optimal" schedule across 400 drivers with dozens of hard constraints and simply using whatever it produces.
questions.question: What is the most sensible approach?

options.A: Ask Claude for the schedule several times and choose the version that looks most balanced, since repeated attempts reduce error.
options.B: Accept Claude's schedule as optimal because language models are good at maths.
options.C: Use Claude to clarify constraints, explain trade-offs and review exceptions, but generate or check the schedule with a tool that tests every constraint.
options.D: Avoid Claude entirely for anything related to scheduling.

questions.explanation: Know where Claude fits in a process. It excels at language, structure and reasoning about trade-offs, but exhaustive constraint checking across hundreds of records needs a deterministic tool or explicit verification.

why_incorrect.A: Picking by appearance does not verify that hard constraints are met.
why_incorrect.B: Large constraint-satisfaction problems need systematic checking; a fluent answer may silently break constraints.
why_incorrect.D: Claude still adds value in clarifying constraints, explaining options and drafting communications.

questions.scenario: Relecloud's customer-success manager wants a better onboarding email sequence for new business customers. She has the current five emails and open-rate data.
questions.question: How can Claude best support the redesign?

options.A: Share the current emails and data, ask for diagnosed weak points and two alternative sequences, then test with a small group.
options.B: Ask Claude to predict the open rate each new email will achieve, so she can pick the strongest sequence before sending anything.
options.C: Ask Claude to write a brand-new sequence without seeing the current one.
options.D: Replace the whole sequence for all new customers with Claude's first redesign, so results are measurable as quickly as possible.

questions.explanation: Solution design with Claude works well as an iterative loop: give it the current state and evidence, ask for options with reasoning, and test before scaling.

why_incorrect.B: Claude cannot reliably predict precise future metrics; testing is needed.
why_incorrect.C: Without the current emails and data, Claude cannot build on what is working or fix what is not.
why_incorrect.D: Rolling out an untested redesign to everyone removes the chance to learn and adjust.

questions.scenario: Adatum Insurance's claims team has designed a new intake form with Claude's help. Before rollout, the team lead wants to find weaknesses in the design.
questions.question: Which use of Claude is most valuable at this stage?

options.A: Ask Claude to confirm that the design meets good-practice standards, so the team has evidence of quality before rollout.
options.B: Ask Claude to add more fields to the form, so that every possible piece of information is captured at intake.
options.C: Ask Claude to add the company logo to every field.
options.D: Ask Claude to critique the design as a first-time claimant, a claims handler and an auditor, listing problems and fixes.

questions.explanation: Claude is useful as a critical reviewer when asked to take specific stakeholder perspectives and identify concrete problems. Framing the request as critique rather than confirmation produces more useful feedback.

why_incorrect.A: Seeking confirmation invites agreement rather than a critical review.
why_incorrect.B: Length is not the goal; a longer form may reduce completion rates.
why_incorrect.C: Branding does not uncover design weaknesses.

questions.scenario: Tailspin Travel's HR team used Claude to draft a new hybrid-working policy. The first draft was well received by managers but employees raised concerns in a pilot survey.
questions.question: Which TWO next steps represent good iteration?

options.A: Ask Claude to rewrite the survey comments in a more constructive, positive tone before sharing them with the policy group.
options.B: Give Claude the survey comments, ask it to group the concerns and suggest specific policy changes for each group.
options.C: Start again from a blank page with a new prompt, so that the second draft is not anchored on the wording of the first.
options.D: Ignore the survey because managers approved the draft.
options.E: Produce a revised draft and a short change log explaining what changed and why, then re-test with a small employee group.

questions.explanation: Iteration uses feedback as input: analyse it, make targeted changes, document what changed and validate again. This keeps what worked and fixes what did not.

why_incorrect.A: Altering feedback hides the problems the iteration is meant to fix.
why_incorrect.C: Discarding the draft throws away the parts managers already supported.
why_incorrect.D: Employee feedback is evidence about whether the policy will work; ignoring it defeats the pilot.

questions.scenario: Bellows College designed a Claude-assisted process in which advisers draft course-recommendation emails for students. After a month, advisers say they spend as long fixing drafts as they used to spend writing.
questions.question: What is the best first step in redesigning the process?

options.A: Sample drafts with advisers' edits, ask Claude to categorise the corrections, and fix the commonest causes.
options.B: Stop the process, since a month of extra editing shows that Claude is not suited to drafting advice for students.
options.C: Ask advisers to send drafts with fewer edits, since small imperfections matter less than the time saved.
options.D: Switch to the most capable model straight away, since drafting quality is mainly determined by model size.

questions.explanation: When a design underperforms, study the evidence. Categorising human corrections reveals whether the problem lies in missing context, unclear instructions or the wrong task split, and points to targeted fixes.

why_incorrect.B: The evidence points to fixable causes; analysing the edits shows what to change.
why_incorrect.C: Sending uncorrected drafts would expose students to errors.
why_incorrect.D: Changing the model without understanding the corrections may not address the real cause.

questions.scenario: Southridge Video's finance team spends hours each month writing commentary on budget variances. The numbers come from a spreadsheet; the commentary follows a standard structure and is reviewed by the finance manager.
questions.question: Which integration approach augments the workflow sensibly?

options.A: Let Claude write the commentary and publish it straight to the board pack, since the numbers come directly from the spreadsheet.
options.B: A Project with the template and style guidance; analysts upload the month's variance table and the manager reviews Claude's draft as before.
options.C: Keep the process fully manual because finance content is too sensitive for any assistance.
options.D: Ask Claude to estimate the variances instead of using the spreadsheet figures.

questions.explanation: Good integration augments existing steps: Claude takes on drafting from authoritative inputs, while existing controls such as manager review stay in place.

why_incorrect.A: Removing the existing review step increases risk for financial reporting.
why_incorrect.C: With appropriate review and data handling, drafting assistance is a common, sensible augmentation.
why_incorrect.D: Estimates would replace accurate source numbers with guesses.

questions.scenario: Northwind Lending's operations team wants to redesign, not just speed up, how it handles internal policy questions from 600 staff. Today, questions arrive by email and two specialists answer them manually.
questions.question: Which TWO design elements are most important in the redesigned workflow?

options.A: Instructing Claude to answer every question even when the policy is silent.
options.B: Removing the two specialists from the process once Claude is available, so their time can be moved to other work and costs fall.
options.C: A shared Project with curated, approved policy documents and instructions to cite the relevant section and refer people to specialists when unsure.
options.D: Letting each staff member upload their own copies of the policies to personal chats, so they can ask questions in the way that suits them.
options.E: An escalation path where unusual or high-impact questions go to the specialists, whose answers then improve the knowledge base.

questions.explanation: Redesigning a workflow means rethinking roles: Claude handles routine questions from curated sources, specialists handle exceptions and maintain the knowledge, and a feedback loop keeps improving the system.

why_incorrect.A: Answering beyond the policy invites invented answers; escalation is safer.
why_incorrect.B: Specialists remain essential for edge cases, accountability and keeping the knowledge base accurate.
why_incorrect.D: Unmanaged copies diverge and lead to inconsistent answers.

questions.scenario: Proseware Education rolled out Claude for drafting parent newsletters. Adoption is low: teachers say it is "one more tool" and they forget to use it.
questions.question: Which change is most likely to improve adoption?

options.A: Send teachers a detailed explainer on how language models work, so they understand the tool well enough to use it.
options.B: Leave adoption to chance and evaluate again next year.
options.C: Require all newsletters to be written entirely by Claude from now on, so that using it becomes the default habit.
options.D: Fit Claude into the existing routine, with a shared Project already set up with the template and examples and a short how-to guide.

questions.explanation: Adoption improves when Claude fits naturally into existing routines, with pre-configured Projects and clear guidance at the point of work, rather than being an extra, separate step.

why_incorrect.A: Background knowledge helps, but the barrier is workflow fit rather than theory.
why_incorrect.B: Without changes, the same barriers will persist.
why_incorrect.C: Mandating full automation ignores teachers' judgement and may reduce quality and trust.

questions.scenario: A team manager at Humongous Insurance asks about the difference between using Claude to augment a workflow and using it to redesign one.
questions.question: Which statement best captures the difference?

options.A: Redesigning means removing human involvement from the process, while augmenting keeps people doing every step.
options.B: There is no difference; both mean adding Claude to a process.
options.C: Augmenting improves existing steps; redesigning rethinks the steps and roles around what Claude and people do best.
options.D: Augmenting means using a smaller, cheaper model; redesigning means moving the work to the most capable model available.

questions.explanation: Augmentation keeps the workflow shape and improves individual steps. Redesign reconsiders which steps exist and who does them, which can unlock larger gains but needs more change management.

why_incorrect.A: Redesign changes roles; human oversight usually remains, especially for important decisions.
why_incorrect.B: They differ in scope: one keeps the process shape, the other changes it.
why_incorrect.D: Model size is unrelated to whether a workflow is augmented or redesigned.

questions.scenario: Fourth Coffee's marketing director asks Aisha whether Claude can "write all our social posts from now on, with no one checking them."
questions.question: Which response communicates value and limitations most accurately?

options.A: No, Claude is not suitable for marketing content, because social posts need a human creative touch that AI cannot provide.
options.B: Claude can draft posts quickly in the brand voice, but a person should check accuracy, tone and timing before publishing.
options.C: Yes, Claude is reliable for marketing content, so once the brand voice is set up the posts can be published as they are.
options.D: Yes, provided the posts stay short, because short posts leave very little room for errors to appear.

questions.explanation: Credible communication about Claude is balanced: state concrete benefits and the specific limitations, along with the controls that manage them.

why_incorrect.A: Understating value ignores clear time savings in drafting.
why_incorrect.C: Overstating reliability sets unrealistic expectations and risks public errors.
why_incorrect.D: Short posts can still contain errors or poor timing; length does not remove the need for review.

questions.scenario: Contoso Health's operations manager is preparing a one-page summary for executives after a three-month Claude pilot in the scheduling team.
questions.question: Which TWO items make the summary most credible?

options.A: Measured results against the baseline, such as average time to draft a schedule notice before and after the pilot.
options.B: Selected positive quotes with negative feedback removed.
options.C: A statement that the model is the most advanced available, as proof of value.
options.D: Projected savings from extending Claude to every department, extrapolated from the scheduling team's results, to show the full opportunity.
options.E: Known limitations seen in the pilot and the controls the team uses to manage them.

questions.explanation: Stakeholders trust evidence: measured outcomes against a baseline, plus an honest account of limitations and how they are handled.

why_incorrect.B: Omitting negative feedback misrepresents the pilot and undermines trust.
why_incorrect.C: Model reputation does not demonstrate value for this team's work.
why_incorrect.D: Untested extrapolation weakens credibility; executives need evidence.

questions.scenario: A frontline team at Acme Logistics fears that Claude will be used to monitor them and replace their jobs. Their manager needs to introduce a Claude pilot for drafting delivery-exception notices.
questions.question: Which communication approach is most appropriate?

options.A: Tell the team that AI will make their roles obsolete, so they should adapt quickly.
options.B: Say nothing about the pilot until it is complete, so the team is not distracted and the results are not influenced.
options.C: Promise the team that nothing about their work or roles will change as a result of the pilot, to reduce anxiety.
options.D: Explain the specific task, what stays with the team (judgement and approval), how data is handled, and invite feedback.

questions.explanation: Transparent, specific communication builds trust: be clear about scope, human responsibilities, data handling and how feedback will be used, without overpromising in either direction.

why_incorrect.A: This is speculative, increases anxiety and misrepresents a narrow drafting pilot.
why_incorrect.B: Secrecy increases mistrust and denies the team a chance to shape the pilot.
why_incorrect.C: An absolute promise is unlikely to be accurate and can damage trust later.

questions.scenario: After a successful pilot, Datum Corp's CFO asks for Claude to be rolled out to the legal team with the claim that it will "eliminate contract errors." The pilot was in marketing.
questions.question: How should the programme lead respond?

options.A: Explain that marketing results do not transfer directly, propose a scoped legal pilot with success measures and review, and drop the error claim.
options.B: Agree to the claim but quietly add reviewers later.
options.C: Decline any legal use, because legal work is too complex for AI and the marketing pilot proves nothing about it.
options.D: Agree, because a successful pilot in one team proves value in all teams.

questions.explanation: Managing expectations means correcting overstatements, separating evidence from extrapolation, and proposing a measured way to test value in the new context.

why_incorrect.B: Accepting an inaccurate claim misleads stakeholders even if controls are added afterwards.
why_incorrect.C: A carefully scoped and reviewed pilot can test value; a blanket refusal is unnecessary.
why_incorrect.D: Different tasks and risk levels mean results must be validated per use case.

questions.scenario: Carmen is setting up a Project at Wingtip Events for writing post-event reports. Every report must use the same section order, a neutral tone and the company's attendance-metric definitions.
questions.question: Where should each piece of information go?

options.A: Put all of it in the first message of each new chat, so that each report starts with a complete and current brief.
options.B: Upload the tone and section guidance as a knowledge file and leave the Project instructions empty, to keep things in one place.
options.C: Section order and tone in the Project instructions; the metric definitions document in Project knowledge.
options.D: Put the metric definitions in Claude's account-level memory.

questions.explanation: Project instructions shape how Claude behaves in every chat in the Project (role, tone, format). Project knowledge holds reference material Claude should draw on. Using each for its purpose keeps the Project predictable.

why_incorrect.A: Repeating set-up in every chat is error-prone; Projects exist to hold this persistently.
why_incorrect.B: Behavioural guidance such as tone and structure belongs in instructions, which tell Claude how to respond in every chat.
why_incorrect.D: Reference material that must be applied exactly belongs in Project knowledge, not in memory that captures selected topics.

questions.scenario: Margie's Travel is creating a shared Project for its 12-person itinerary team on a Team plan. A senior planner will maintain it.
questions.question: Which TWO configuration choices are sound?

options.A: Give the senior planner "Can edit" access and most members "Can view" access, so they can chat but not change the set-up.
options.B: Give every team member edit access, so that anyone who finds a useful supplier document can add it to the knowledge straight away.
options.C: Upload every itinerary from the past ten years, so Claude has the widest possible set of examples to draw on for new trips.
options.D: Leave the instructions blank so each planner can phrase their own each time.
options.E: Upload only current, approved supplier guides and itinerary templates to the Project knowledge.

questions.explanation: On Team and Enterprise plans, Projects can be shared with view or edit permissions. Restricting edit rights to an owner and curating knowledge to current, relevant material keeps a shared Project reliable.

why_incorrect.B: Uncontrolled edits lead to conflicting or outdated knowledge and inconsistent answers.
why_incorrect.C: Bulk uploads of loosely relevant material add noise and make answers less focused.
why_incorrect.D: Shared instructions are what make outputs consistent across the team.

questions.scenario: Jamal at Trey Research uploaded a 400-page set of research reports to a Project on a paid plan. Claude still answers questions using the material but now seems to draw on a few relevant passages rather than the whole set at once.
questions.question: What is the most likely explanation?

options.A: Projects only read the first section of each file, so long reports need to be split into many smaller uploads.
options.B: Knowledge near the context limit made the Project switch to retrieval, which finds the relevant passages.
options.C: The upload partly failed, so Claude can only see some of the reports and is filling the gaps from general knowledge.
options.D: Claude ignores Project knowledge whenever memory is turned on.

questions.explanation: As of 2026-10-24, on paid plans, when Project knowledge approaches the context limit Claude automatically uses retrieval to find relevant parts of the knowledge, which expands capacity. Clear, well-structured documents help retrieval find the right passages.

why_incorrect.A: There is no rule that Projects read only the first section of files; large knowledge bases are handled through retrieval on paid plans.
why_incorrect.C: Claude is answering accurately from the reports, which points to retrieval selecting passages rather than a failed upload.
why_incorrect.D: Memory and Project knowledge are separate features; memory does not disable knowledge.

questions.scenario: Bellows College's admissions office plans one Project for both undergraduate and postgraduate enquiries. The two have different deadlines, fees and tone requirements, and staff keep getting answers that mix them up.
questions.question: What is the best configuration change?

options.A: Use a standalone chat without a Project for every enquiry.
options.B: Keep one Project and add an instruction to "be careful to use the correct programme's information" in every answer.
options.C: Keep one Project and remove all fee documents to avoid mistakes.
options.D: Create separate Projects for undergraduate and postgraduate enquiries, each with its own instructions and knowledge.

questions.explanation: Projects work best when scoped to a coherent body of work. When two audiences need different rules and facts, separate Projects prevent cross-contamination and make each easier to maintain.

why_incorrect.A: This loses the persistent instructions and knowledge entirely.
why_incorrect.B: A vague instruction does not stop Claude drawing on the wrong set of fees and deadlines.
why_incorrect.C: Removing needed information makes the Project less useful rather than more accurate.

questions.scenario: Isabel at Fabrikam Retail uses the Gmail connector and asks Claude to summarise the PDF invoices attached to supplier emails from last week. Claude lists the emails and attachment names but cannot summarise the invoice contents.
questions.question: What is the most likely reason?

options.A: Gmail exposes message content and attachment metadata, not attachment contents; she should add the PDFs to the chat directly.
options.B: Invoice PDFs need a more capable model to interpret tables, so she should switch models and ask again.
options.C: The Gmail connector has lost its authorisation, so it can see email headers but not files; she should disconnect and reconnect it.
options.D: Claude cannot read any PDF in any context.

questions.explanation: As of 2026-10-24, the Gmail connector exposes message content and attachment metadata, not attachment contents. Knowing each connector's scope helps users pick the right route for the data they need.

why_incorrect.B: Model choice does not change what data the connector makes available.
why_incorrect.C: Listing emails and attachment names shows it is working within its normal scope.
why_incorrect.D: Claude can read PDFs uploaded directly or retrieved from supported sources such as Drive.

questions.scenario: Tom at Alpine Ski House wants a private Project to always use the latest version of the team's pricing guide, which colleagues edit in Google Docs.
questions.question: What is the best approach?

options.A: Ask colleagues to email him changes so he can tell Claude about them.
options.B: Download a PDF of the guide on the first of each month and upload it to the Project, deleting the previous copy each time.
options.C: Add the Google Doc from Google Drive, so Claude uses the latest synced version.
options.D: Copy the full text of the guide into the Project instructions, so Claude always reads it before answering.

questions.explanation: Google Docs added to chats and Projects through the Drive connector sync from Drive, so Claude uses the latest version. As of 2026-10-24, adding Drive files to Project knowledge is available for private Projects.

why_incorrect.A: This is slow, error-prone and depends on people remembering to send updates.
why_incorrect.B: Manual re-uploads can be forgotten and create stale copies, while a Drive-linked Doc stays current.
why_incorrect.D: Instructions are for guidance on behaviour; pasted reference text goes stale and bloats the instructions.

questions.scenario: Northwind Lending, on an Enterprise plan, is enabling the Google Drive connector for the first time.
questions.question: Which TWO statements about access and administration are accurate?

options.A: Once one administrator connects their Google account, every member can search every file in the company Drive through Claude.
options.B: An organisation Owner must enable the connector before members can connect their own Google accounts.
options.C: Content from connected Drive files is automatically copied into the shared knowledge of every Project in the organisation.
options.D: The connector respects each user's existing Google permissions, so Claude can only reach files that user can access.
options.E: Users can bypass the Owner setting by installing the connector in a personal browser.

questions.explanation: As of 2026-10-24, on Team and Enterprise plans an Owner enables Google Workspace connectors first; then each member authenticates with their own account, and Claude's access mirrors that user's Google permissions.

why_incorrect.A: Each user authenticates individually and access mirrors their own Google permissions.
why_incorrect.C: Connector content is pulled into the chats and Projects where it is used; it is not automatically copied into every Project.
why_incorrect.E: Organisation controls govern connector availability for members on Team and Enterprise plans.

questions.scenario: Claude summarised a Google Slides deck from Drive for Wei at Southridge Video, but missed all the numbers shown in the embedded chart images.
questions.question: What explains this, and what should Wei do?

options.A: The Drive connector extracts text only, so embedded images are skipped; provide the figures as text or upload the charts.
options.B: Claude declines to report numbers from presentations, to avoid misquoting financial data, so the figures must be typed in.
options.C: The deck is too long; split it into one-slide files.
options.D: Slides files can only be read in part through the Drive connector, so Wei should export the deck to Word first.

questions.explanation: As of 2026-10-24, the Drive connector reads text from supported files and does not process images embedded in documents. Knowing this helps users spot gaps and supply missing visual data another way.

why_incorrect.B: There is no such refusal; the issue is how content is extracted from Drive files.
why_incorrect.C: Length is not the cause; images would still be skipped in shorter files.
why_incorrect.D: Slides text is read; only the embedded images are skipped.

questions.scenario: Rosa is writing Project instructions for Coho Winery's sales team. Her draft says: "Be helpful and professional."
questions.question: Which revision makes the instructions most effective?

options.A: Add "be very, very helpful" for emphasis.
options.B: Replace it with a detailed list of words, phrases and topics Claude must never use with customers.
options.C: State the users, supported tasks, tone and format, which knowledge files to rely on, and what to do when information is missing.
options.D: Leave it as is; Claude will infer everything else.

questions.explanation: Strong system-level instructions explain the context and the expected behaviour: audience, purpose, style, sources and how to handle uncertainty. Specific guidance produces consistent results across chats.

why_incorrect.A: Emphasis does not add the missing context about users, tasks or format.
why_incorrect.B: A banned-word list ignores the core guidance on role, tasks and format.
why_incorrect.D: Without specifics, outputs will vary from chat to chat and person to person.

questions.scenario: Lucerne Clinics' HR team is writing instructions for a Project that answers staff questions about leave policies using uploaded policy documents.
questions.question: Which THREE instructions are most appropriate?

options.A: If the documents are unclear, choose the interpretation most favourable to the employee.
options.B: Answer only from the uploaded policy documents and name the policy and section used.
options.C: Never mention that answers come from documents, so they sound authoritative.
options.D: If the documents do not cover a question, say so and direct the person to the HR inbox.
options.E: Use plain language and keep answers under 150 words unless the person asks for more detail.

questions.explanation: Effective instructions define the source of truth, the behaviour when the source is silent, and the expected format. Escalating uncertain cases and citing sources keeps answers verifiable.

why_incorrect.A: Resolving ambiguity on Claude's own judgement can produce inconsistent, unauthorised answers; unclear cases should be escalated.
why_incorrect.C: Hiding sources makes answers harder to verify and undermines trust.

questions.scenario: Tailspin Travel's Project instructions contain both "Always respond in bullet points" and, later, "Write responses as flowing paragraphs suitable for emails." Outputs alternate unpredictably between the two.
questions.question: What is the best fix?

options.A: Delete the instructions entirely and specify format in each chat.
options.B: Add a further instruction telling Claude to choose whichever format best suits each request, so it can resolve the conflict itself.
options.C: Move the bullet-point rule to the top of the instructions, because the earliest instruction is the one Claude gives priority.
options.D: State when each format applies, for example bullets for internal notes and paragraphs for customer emails.

questions.explanation: Contradictory instructions produce inconsistent results. Review instructions for conflicts and make conditions explicit so Claude knows which rule applies in which situation.

why_incorrect.A: This removes useful shared guidance instead of fixing the conflict.
why_incorrect.B: This leaves the conflict unresolved and the outputs still unpredictable.
why_incorrect.C: Reordering does not clarify intent; both rules still apply to the same situations.

questions.scenario: A manager at Humongous Insurance asks why her Project instructions explain the reasons behind rules, such as "Avoid jargon because most readers are new policyholders", instead of just listing the rules.
questions.question: What is the main benefit of giving reasons?

options.A: Reasons are needed only for legal compliance documentation.
options.B: Knowing why a rule exists helps Claude apply it sensibly in situations the rule did not anticipate.
options.C: Reasons make instructions longer and more detailed, and longer instructions consistently produce better results.
options.D: Claude tends to ignore rules that have no reason attached, so every rule needs a justification to be followed.

questions.explanation: Explaining the purpose behind an instruction lets Claude generalise it correctly, for example simplifying technical terms in a new kind of document because it understands who the readers are.

why_incorrect.A: The benefit is better application of the rule, not documentation.
why_incorrect.C: Length alone does not improve results; the value comes from the context reasons provide.
why_incorrect.D: Claude follows clear rules without reasons; reasons improve judgement in edge cases.

questions.scenario: Acme Logistics' shared customs-guidance Project has grown over a year. Several team members have uploaded slightly different versions of the same export checklist, and answers sometimes quote different requirements.
questions.question: What should the Project owner do?

options.A: Keep one approved, dated version of the checklist, remove the duplicates, and agree who may update it.
options.B: Delete the Project and start a new one each quarter.
options.C: Add an instruction telling Claude to combine the requirements from all the versions, so no requirement is missed.
options.D: Leave all versions in the knowledge, so Claude can compare them and choose the most complete one for each answer.

questions.explanation: Knowledge needs curation. One approved, dated version per document, plus clear ownership of changes, keeps answers consistent.

why_incorrect.B: Rebuilding regularly loses useful configuration and does not fix the version-control problem.
why_incorrect.C: Combining conflicting versions can produce requirements the approved checklist does not contain; the fix is one approved version.
why_incorrect.D: Conflicting versions in knowledge cause conflicting answers; Claude cannot know which is approved.

questions.scenario: Woodgrove Bank's operations team relies on six shared Projects. The team lead wants a lightweight maintenance routine.
questions.question: Which TWO practices should the routine include?

options.A: Allow anyone on the team to edit instructions at any time without notice, so improvements reach everyone as quickly as possible.
options.B: Review Projects only when a serious error has reached a customer.
options.C: A named owner for each Project who reviews instructions and knowledge on a regular schedule, such as quarterly.
options.D: Add every new document the team receives to every Project automatically, so that the knowledge in each Project stays complete.
options.E: A small set of standard test questions run after each significant change to confirm answers are still correct.

questions.explanation: Ownership, scheduled reviews and simple regression checks with known questions are effective ways to keep configurations reliable as content and needs change.

why_incorrect.A: Unmanaged edits make behaviour change unexpectedly and are hard to trace.
why_incorrect.B: Purely reactive maintenance lets errors reach people before they are caught.
why_incorrect.D: Indiscriminate additions dilute knowledge and introduce conflicts.

questions.scenario: Graphic Design Institute's student-services team changed its Project instructions to make answers shorter. Afterwards, answers are shorter but no longer include the link to the booking system, which used to appear every time.
questions.question: What is the most likely cause, and the best fix?

options.A: Shorter answers cannot contain links, so the team must choose between brevity and including the booking link.
options.B: The booking system may be offline, and Claude stops mentioning links to systems that are unavailable.
options.C: The edit weakened the booking-link instruction; restore it explicitly and re-run standard test questions after each change.
options.D: The Project knowledge was automatically deleted.

questions.explanation: Changes to instructions can have unintended side effects. Compare the old and new versions, restore the lost requirement and test with a standard question set after every edit.

why_incorrect.A: Short answers can include links if instructed.
why_incorrect.B: Claude is not checking the system's status; the change coincides with the instruction edit.
why_incorrect.D: Knowledge does not disappear because of an instruction edit; the instructions changed.

questions.scenario: Relecloud's sales team installed a custom Skill from an external website six months ago. A new version is now available from the same site, and the team wants to install it immediately.
questions.question: What is the most responsible maintenance step?

options.A: Disable code execution permanently to avoid any Skill risk.
options.B: Review the new version's files, instructions and external connections before enabling it.
options.C: Enable it for the whole organisation first, then ask users to report anything unusual over the following week.
options.D: Install it straight away, because the earlier version from the same site has worked safely for six months.

questions.explanation: Skills can include instructions and code that influence Claude's actions. Treat updates from less-trusted sources like new software: review the contents, check for unexpected network access, and only then enable them.

why_incorrect.A: Skills rely on code execution; a blanket disable removes their benefit instead of managing the risk.
why_incorrect.C: Broad rollout before review spreads any risk across all users.
why_incorrect.D: A previous version being safe does not guarantee the new one is; each version should be reviewed.

questions.scenario: Adatum Insurance's team is listing possible Claude uses: drafting internal training quizzes, summarising public industry reports, brainstorming event themes, and automatically deciding which claims are denied with no human involvement.
questions.question: Which proposed use is most clearly inappropriate as described?

options.A: Brainstorming themes and session titles for the annual customer event.
options.B: Drafting internal training quizzes on claims procedures for new staff.
options.C: Summarising public industry reports on claims trends for the leadership team.
options.D: Automatically deciding claim denials with no human involvement.

questions.explanation: Decisions with significant consequences for individuals, such as insurance claim denials, should not be fully automated without human oversight. Anthropic's Usage Policy sets additional requirements for high-risk uses that affect people's access to services, including human review.

why_incorrect.A: Brainstorming is low-stakes and benefits from Claude's creativity.
why_incorrect.B: This is a low-risk drafting task where a human can easily check the result.
why_incorrect.C: Summarising public material is a standard, low-risk use, with normal accuracy checks.

questions.scenario: Proseware Education's teachers are discussing ways to use Claude with students' work.
questions.question: Which TWO uses are appropriate, assuming school policy allows them?

options.A: Generating varied practice questions on a topic for revision.
options.B: Writing essays for students to submit as their own work.
options.C: Asking Claude to determine whether a student is lying about being ill.
options.D: Assigning final grades automatically to save teacher time, with teachers reading only essays that Claude marks as borderline.
options.E: Drafting general feedback themes on a set of anonymised essays, which the teacher then reviews and personalises.

questions.explanation: Appropriate uses support people's judgement and are easy to check, such as practice material and draft feedback. Inappropriate uses hand consequential judgements to Claude or enable dishonesty.

why_incorrect.B: This undermines academic integrity and the purpose of assessment.
why_incorrect.C: Claude cannot reliably make such a judgement, and using it this way could unfairly harm the student.
why_incorrect.D: Final grading has real consequences for students and needs the teacher's judgement.

questions.scenario: A recruiter at Datum Corp wants to paste 200 CVs into Claude and ask it to "reject anyone who doesn't seem like a culture fit."
questions.question: What is the best response?

options.A: Ask Claude to infer candidates' ages from graduation years to help screening.
options.B: Proceed as asked, because Claude applies the same standard to every CV and is therefore free from the biases people have.
options.C: Reframe it: summarise CVs against defined, job-related criteria, with a recruiter making and recording decisions.
options.D: Proceed, but start with the first 50 CVs and review a few rejections to see whether the results look sensible.

questions.explanation: Employment decisions are high-impact. Use clear, job-related criteria, keep humans accountable for decisions, and avoid vague criteria or inferences about protected characteristics.

why_incorrect.A: Inferring protected characteristics for screening creates discrimination risk.
why_incorrect.B: Models can reflect biases, and "culture fit" is a vague criterion that can mask discrimination.
why_incorrect.D: Reducing the number does not address the inappropriate criterion or lack of human decision-making.

questions.scenario: Fourth Coffee's social media lead asks Claude to write 50 five-star customer reviews to post on review sites under made-up names for a new store.
questions.question: Why is this inappropriate, and what is a better alternative?

options.A: It is inappropriate only because 50 is too many; five would be fine.
options.B: Fake reviews deceive consumers and breach usage policies; instead, invite genuine customers to leave honest reviews.
options.C: It is acceptable if each review is written in a different style, so the reviews read as natural and varied.
options.D: It is acceptable as long as the reviews are well written and describe things the store genuinely offers.

questions.explanation: Using Claude to create deceptive content, such as fake reviews presented as genuine, is inappropriate. Claude can instead support honest approaches that achieve the same business goal.

why_incorrect.A: Any number of fabricated reviews is deceptive.
why_incorrect.C: Variety makes the deception harder to spot, not acceptable.
why_incorrect.D: Even accurate descriptions are deceptive when presented as reviews from customers who do not exist.

questions.scenario: A new employee at Coho Winery asks how to tell whether a task is a good fit for Claude.
questions.question: Which rule of thumb is most useful?

options.A: Tasks are a good fit only if Claude can complete them without any human involvement.
options.B: Any task is a good fit as long as it saves a meaningful amount of time compared with doing it by hand.
options.C: Only tasks that involve numbers or data are a good fit, since writing tasks depend too much on personal judgement.
options.D: Tasks where the output can be checked and errors are manageable, or where a human makes the final call.

questions.explanation: Assess fit by verifiability, consequence of errors and the presence of human decision-making, not only by convenience.

why_incorrect.A: Many of the best uses combine Claude's drafting with human judgement.
why_incorrect.B: Time saved does not justify uses that are high-risk, deceptive or impossible to verify.
why_incorrect.C: Writing is one of Claude's main strengths.

questions.scenario: Lena, a team manager at Lucerne Clinics, wants Claude to help rewrite a sick-leave summary that contains staff names and medical diagnoses. Her organisation has an approved Claude Enterprise workspace and a policy on health data.
questions.question: What should she do first?

options.A: Check the policy on health data; if allowed, use only the approved workspace, otherwise remove identifying details first.
options.B: Ask Claude whether it is permitted to process health data, and follow its answer, since it knows its own data handling.
options.C: Paste it anywhere, because Claude does not store anything.
options.D: Paste it into her personal free account, which is quicker, and delete the chat afterwards so nothing is kept.

questions.explanation: Health information is highly sensitive. Follow organisational policy, use the approved environment, and minimise or de-identify data where possible.

why_incorrect.B: Claude cannot know her organisation's policies; the policy owner decides.
why_incorrect.C: Data handling depends on the account, settings and policies; it is not safe to assume nothing is retained.
why_incorrect.D: Personal accounts may not have the organisation's contractual and administrative protections for sensitive data.

questions.scenario: Northwind Lending's marketing team wants to use Claude to analyse customer feedback that includes names, email addresses and free-text comments.
questions.question: Which TWO practices best reduce privacy risk while keeping the analysis useful?

options.A: Share the analysis chat publicly so other teams can learn from it.
options.B: Remove names and email addresses before analysis, since themes do not depend on identity.
options.C: Use the organisation's approved Claude workspace that is covered by its data agreements.
options.D: Ask Claude to look up each customer's social media profiles to enrich the analysis.
options.E: Keep all identifiers in the data, so Claude can link related comments from the same customer and personalise each finding.

questions.explanation: Data minimisation and approved environments are core privacy practices: share only what the task needs, and use tools covered by the organisation's agreements and controls.

why_incorrect.A: Publicly sharing a chat containing customer data could expose personal information.
why_incorrect.D: Compiling extra personal data goes beyond the purpose and increases privacy risk.
why_incorrect.E: Identifiers add risk without improving theme analysis.

questions.scenario: Woodgrove Bank's strategy team is evaluating a confidential acquisition. An analyst wants to use the research feature with connectors to Drive and Gmail to gather everything related to the target company.
questions.question: What is the most important consideration?

options.A: Connect every available connector, so the research is as complete as possible and nothing relevant to the target is missed.
options.B: Confirm policy allows it, use the approved workspace, and connect only the needed sources, since research reads whatever they can access.
options.C: Use a personal account for the research, which keeps the confidential deal details away from the bank's shared systems.
options.D: Paste the deal details into a public forum to get more opinions.

questions.explanation: Connectors give Claude access to data in connected accounts. Limit connections to what is needed and keep confidential work in approved, governed environments.

why_incorrect.A: Broad connector access exposes more confidential data than the task needs.
why_incorrect.C: Avoiding organisational oversight for confidential work is a policy and security violation.
why_incorrect.D: Public disclosure of confidential deal information is a serious breach.

questions.scenario: A Graphic Design Institute administrator in the EU wants Claude to draft letters to students using enrolment data. Their data protection officer asks about lawful processing.
questions.question: Which approach is most appropriate?

options.A: Work with the data protection officer on purpose, legal basis and minimum data, then use only an approved account.
options.B: Proceed only if Claude confirms that the processing is lawful under the relevant data protection rules.
options.C: Send the full enrolment database, so the letters can be as personalised and accurate as possible.
options.D: Proceed, because drafting letters is a routine administrative task and does not count as processing personal data.

questions.explanation: Regulatory requirements apply to AI-assisted processing like any other. Involve accountable roles, confirm purpose and legal basis, minimise data and use approved tools.

why_incorrect.B: Legal determinations belong to the organisation's accountable roles, not to Claude.
why_incorrect.C: Sending more data than needed conflicts with data minimisation.
why_incorrect.D: Using enrolment data to draft letters is processing personal data, and data protection obligations apply whatever tool is used.

questions.scenario: Tom at Acme Logistics asks whether there is anything he should never paste into Claude, even in the approved company workspace.
questions.question: Which answer best reflects good practice?

options.A: Only images are risky; text is always safe.
options.B: Only data older than five years is safe to share.
options.C: Anything is fine in the approved workspace, including system passwords, because the workspace is covered by company agreements.
options.D: Never paste secrets such as passwords, keys or tokens, and follow policy for other restricted data.

questions.explanation: Some information, such as credentials, should never be entered into a chat. Other categories depend on policy, environment and need.

why_incorrect.A: Text can contain highly sensitive information.
why_incorrect.B: The age of data does not determine its sensitivity.
why_incorrect.C: Credentials should never be shared in chat; their exposure can lead to account compromise.

questions.scenario: Southridge Video's AI policy requires staff to use the company's Claude Team workspace for work and to label AI-assisted public content. Ben prefers his personal account because he has his own Projects set up there.
questions.question: What should Ben do?

options.A: Use his personal account only for the most confidential work, where keeping things separate from shared systems matters most.
options.B: Keep using his personal account for work, since his Projects are already set up there and the outputs are the same.
options.C: Recreate the Projects in the company workspace without copying restricted data, and follow the labelling rule.
options.D: Ask a colleague to approve an exception informally over chat.

questions.explanation: Organisational AI policies define approved tools and practices. Follow them, and use formal exception routes when there is a genuine need.

why_incorrect.A: Confidential work is exactly what should stay in the governed workspace.
why_incorrect.B: Convenience does not override policy; personal accounts sit outside company controls.
why_incorrect.D: Exceptions should go through the policy's formal process, not informal approval.

questions.scenario: Fabrikam Retail is writing its first AI usage policy for Claude across business teams.
questions.question: Which THREE elements should the policy include?

options.A: A requirement that staff never mention AI use to customers under any circumstances, to protect the company's brand.
options.B: Which tools and plans are approved for work use.
options.C: A rule that the most capable available model must always be used for every task, so quality never depends on individual choices.
options.D: Data classifications that may or may not be used with Claude, with examples.
options.E: Human review requirements for AI-assisted output, by risk level.

questions.explanation: Effective AI policies cover approved tools, data handling rules and review requirements scaled to risk, along with clear ownership and an exception process.

why_incorrect.A: Blanket concealment conflicts with transparency expectations and some disclosure obligations.
why_incorrect.C: Model choice is a task-level decision, not a governance requirement.

questions.scenario: An audit at Humongous Insurance finds that several teams uploaded customer complaint files to Projects shared with the whole organisation, although policy restricts them to the complaints team.
questions.question: What is the best corrective action?

options.A: Limit sharing to the complaints team, remove files where not allowed, report it, and reinforce training.
options.B: Ask Claude in each Project to forget the complaint files so they are no longer used.
options.C: Take no action, since only employees had access and nothing left the organisation.
options.D: Delete every Project across the organisation and start again with stricter rules.

questions.explanation: Governance failures need containment (fix access), correction (remove data where it does not belong), reporting and prevention (training and configuration).

why_incorrect.B: Access is controlled by sharing settings and file management, not by asking Claude.
why_incorrect.C: Internal over-sharing still breaches the policy and can expose customers' data.
why_incorrect.D: This is disproportionate and destroys legitimate work.

questions.scenario: Margie's Travel's IT owner is deciding whether members on the company's Enterprise plan may let Claude send emails through the Gmail connector without approving each message.
questions.question: Which approach best aligns with good governance?

options.A: Allow automatic sending for all members, since the Enterprise plan already provides strong security and it saves time.
options.B: Let each user decide without any guidance.
options.C: Keep per-action approval for sending as the default, relaxing it only for reviewed, low-risk uses.
options.D: Disable every connector permanently, since any connector that can act on email is too risky to allow.

questions.explanation: As of 2026-10-24, Owners can control whether members may run send, share, move and trash actions without per-action approval. Keeping human confirmation for actions with external effects is a sensible default.

why_incorrect.A: Removing approval for outbound communication increases the risk of mistaken or manipulated messages.
why_incorrect.B: Unguided individual choices produce inconsistent risk across the organisation.
why_incorrect.D: This forgoes legitimate read-only benefits; governance can manage the risk proportionately.

questions.scenario: A manager at Contoso Health asks who is responsible when a report drafted with Claude contains an error that reaches a client.
questions.question: Which statement reflects sound governance?

options.A: Nobody can be held responsible, because errors from AI tools are unpredictable by nature.
options.B: The client is responsible, because recipients are expected to check anything they rely on.
options.C: Anthropic is responsible for errors in Claude's outputs, since the model generated the content.
options.D: The people who used and approved the output remain accountable, which is why review matters.

questions.explanation: AI assistance does not transfer accountability. Governance assigns ownership for outputs and requires proportionate review before they are used.

why_incorrect.A: Unpredictability is a reason for review, not a removal of accountability.
why_incorrect.B: The sender is accountable for what they send.
why_incorrect.C: Organisations remain responsible for how they use and approve outputs.

questions.scenario: Wingtip Events used Claude to draft a keynote speech for its CEO. A journalist later asks whether AI was used.
questions.question: Which response is most ethical?

options.A: Explain that the speech was written entirely by AI, so the CEO should not be held responsible for any of its content.
options.B: Answer honestly that AI helped draft the speech and the CEO reviewed and owns it, in line with policy.
options.C: Refuse to comment and delete the drafts.
options.D: Say that the CEO wrote the speech personally, since the CEO approved the final text and AI help is an internal detail.

questions.explanation: Transparency about AI assistance, alongside clear human ownership of the content, supports trust.

why_incorrect.A: This is inaccurate and disowns responsibility for the content.
why_incorrect.C: Destroying records to avoid scrutiny is not transparent.
why_incorrect.D: Lying about AI use is deceptive and risks reputational harm if discovered.

questions.scenario: Tailspin Travel's marketing team wants to use Claude to produce persuasive campaign copy.
questions.question: Which TWO practices reflect ethical use?

options.A: Make sure claims are truthful and substantiated, and avoid exploiting customers' fears or vulnerabilities.
options.B: Write copy that imitates a competitor's brand so customers confuse the two.
options.C: Use Claude to generate fake scarcity messages, such as "only 2 seats left" when that is untrue.
options.D: Remove the small-print disclaimers from offers, so that the main message is clearer and the ads look more appealing.
options.E: Review copy for stereotypes or exclusionary language before publishing.

questions.explanation: Persuasion is legitimate when it is honest and respectful. Ethical use means truthful claims, no manipulation and inclusive language.

why_incorrect.B: Deliberately confusing customers is deceptive and may infringe rights.
why_incorrect.C: Fabricated scarcity is deceptive and manipulates customers.
why_incorrect.D: Removing required disclaimers misleads customers.

questions.scenario: Litware Publishing's editor wants to use Claude to write a book chapter "in the exact style" of a living novelist and publish it under the editor's name as original work.
questions.question: What is the main ethical concern, and the better path?

options.A: The concern is cost, because long chapters use more of the usage allowance.
options.B: There is no concern, because a writing style cannot be owned and Claude produces new sentences rather than copying text.
options.C: Close imitation of a living author passed off as original raises authorship and IP concerns; develop an original voice instead.
options.D: The only concern is length; shorter chapters are fine.

questions.explanation: Using AI to imitate a specific living creator and present the result as original work raises ethical and legal questions. Original creation and honest attribution avoid them.

why_incorrect.A: Usage is not the ethical issue.
why_incorrect.B: Close imitation presented as original still raises authorship and possible infringement issues.
why_incorrect.D: The concern is authenticity and intellectual property, not length.

questions.scenario: Datum Corp's analyst asks Claude, with the web browsing and research tools on, to summarise a supplier's public web page. The page contains hidden text instructing AI assistants to say the supplier has perfect safety records.
questions.question: What does this illustrate, and how should the analyst respond?

options.A: Indirect prompt injection; treat external content as untrusted, check the summary against other sources, and report it.
options.B: It shows that research should never be used.
options.C: Nothing to act on, because Claude reliably detects and ignores hidden instructions in web pages it reads.
options.D: A harmless formatting issue on the supplier's site, so the summary can be used once the odd text is ignored.

questions.explanation: Content retrieved from the web or connected sources can contain instructions intended to manipulate AI output. Treat it as untrusted, verify important claims and report attempts.

why_incorrect.B: The risk is managed through verification and caution, not by abandoning useful tools.
why_incorrect.C: Defences reduce risk but are not perfect; human verification still matters.
why_incorrect.D: Hidden instructions aimed at AI are a manipulation attempt, not a formatting issue.

questions.scenario: Bellows College's ethics committee asks why over-reliance on AI tools is an ethical issue and not only a quality issue.
questions.question: Which answer is most accurate?

options.A: Over-reliance is impossible because AI is always correct.
options.B: It can erode human skills and judgement, hide errors that affect people, and blur accountability.
options.C: Over-reliance is mainly a cost issue, because heavy use of AI tools increases subscription and usage spending.
options.D: Over-reliance matters mainly for technical staff, who might lose coding skills if they rely on AI assistants.

questions.explanation: Responsible use keeps humans engaged and accountable. Over-reliance can let errors affect people unnoticed and weaken the human judgement that oversight depends on.

why_incorrect.A: AI is not always correct; that is part of the concern.
why_incorrect.C: The concern is about people, fairness and accountability, not only cost.
why_incorrect.D: Any role that depends on AI output can be affected.

questions.scenario: Claude keeps writing 800-word answers for Joel at Relecloud when he wants a few sentences. His prompt says, "Don't be too wordy."
questions.question: What is the most effective fix?

options.A: Ask Claude to explain why its answers are so long, so it becomes aware of the problem and adjusts.
options.B: Repeat "don't be wordy" several times in the prompt so that the instruction carries more weight.
options.C: Switch to the most capable model, which is better at judging the right length for each question.
options.D: Say concretely what you want: "Answer in three sentences or fewer."

questions.explanation: Vague or negative instructions leave room for interpretation. Saying what you want, with a concrete measure, is more reliable than saying what to avoid.

why_incorrect.A: An explanation does not change the next output; a clear instruction does.
why_incorrect.B: Repetition does not define what length is acceptable.
why_incorrect.C: Model choice does not fix an unclear length requirement.

questions.scenario: Claude's weekly sales summaries for VanArsdel Foods are inconsistent: sometimes a table, sometimes prose, and regional figures are occasionally missing.
questions.question: Which TWO prompt changes target the root causes?

options.A: Use a fresh chat each day, so that earlier summaries in the conversation do not influence the structure of the new one.
options.B: Add a line asking Claude to be more consistent this week and to keep the same style as the previous summaries.
options.C: Specify an exact output structure, for example a table with fixed columns and a three-bullet commentary.
options.D: Remove the regional breakdown from the input, so Claude has less data to handle and the summary is simpler and more uniform.
options.E: List the required regions explicitly and ask Claude to write "no data" when a region is missing from the input.

questions.explanation: Inconsistent format comes from an unspecified structure; missing items come from unstated completeness requirements. Specify both explicitly, including how to handle gaps.

why_incorrect.A: Changing chats does not define format or completeness.
why_incorrect.B: A general request does not define what consistency means.
why_incorrect.D: Removing data makes the summary less complete, not more.

questions.scenario: A Contoso Health analyst asks Claude in a Project to answer questions from uploaded clinic procedures. Claude sometimes answers from general knowledge instead of the procedures, giving advice that differs from local practice.
questions.question: What is the best fix?

options.A: In the Project instructions, require answers only from the procedures, with quotes, and a clear note when they do not cover the question.
options.B: Ask questions in shorter sentences.
options.C: Upload general medical reference textbooks as well, so Claude has a fuller picture and relies less on its own general knowledge.
options.D: Turn on memory so that, over time, Claude learns the clinic's procedures from the questions staff ask.

questions.explanation: When answers must reflect specific documents, say so explicitly, require quotes and give Claude permission to say the documents do not cover something. This reduces reliance on general knowledge.

why_incorrect.B: Question length does not determine which source Claude relies on.
why_incorrect.C: More general material increases the chance of answers that differ from local procedures.
why_incorrect.D: Memory does not replace explicit grounding in the approved documents.

questions.scenario: Claude drafts excellent first-round interview summaries for Northwind Lending's HR team, but consistently rates every candidate as a "strong hire", even when the interviewer's notes are negative.
questions.question: What is the most likely cause, and the best fix?

options.A: The interview notes are too long, so Claude reads only the opening section, which tends to be positive.
options.B: No rating rubric was defined; give criteria with examples per level and ask Claude to cite the notes behind each rating.
options.C: A faster model would be less generous, because slower models spend more effort finding positives.
options.D: Claude is designed to describe people positively, so it cannot give negative assessments of candidates.

questions.explanation: Ratings drift towards generic positivity when standards are undefined. A rubric with examples for each level, plus evidence for each rating, anchors judgements in the notes. Humans still make the hiring decision.

why_incorrect.A: The summaries are otherwise accurate, so the notes are being read.
why_incorrect.C: Speed does not affect leniency; criteria do.
why_incorrect.D: Claude can give critical assessments when given clear criteria; the gap is the missing rubric.

questions.scenario: A team lead at Alpine Ski House wants a quick checklist for diagnosing a poor Claude response.
questions.question: Which first question is most useful?

options.A: Is the model having a technical problem today, and would trying again later give a better response?
options.B: Was the response long enough to cover the topic in sufficient detail?
options.C: Did I phrase the request politely enough for Claude to make its best effort?
options.D: Did my prompt give Claude the context, task, format and constraints it needed?

questions.explanation: Most underperformance traces back to the prompt or inputs. Checking for missing context, unclear tasks, unspecified formats and unstated constraints resolves the majority of issues.

why_incorrect.A: Outages are rare; most poor outputs trace to missing context or unclear instructions.
why_incorrect.B: Length is only one aspect and may not be the problem at all.
why_incorrect.C: Politeness is fine but does not supply missing requirements.

questions.scenario: Readers of Fabrikam Retail's internal newsletter, drafted with Claude, say the articles are too formal. The editor wants to adjust.
questions.question: What is the best next step?

options.A: Stop using Claude for the newsletter, since a tone problem shows it cannot match the company's culture.
options.B: Keep the formal style, because it is safer for company-wide communication and readers will adjust to it over time.
options.C: Update the instructions with the new tone guidance and examples, then check the next issue against reader feedback.
options.D: Ask readers to get used to the formal style.

questions.explanation: Feedback should change the configuration that produces the output. Updating instructions with examples and checking the effect closes the loop.

why_incorrect.A: The tone is adjustable; abandoning the tool is unnecessary.
why_incorrect.B: The goal is a newsletter people read; feedback indicates a gap.
why_incorrect.D: This places the burden on readers rather than fixing the output.

questions.scenario: Coho Winery's tasting-room team has used a Claude-drafted visitor FAQ for a month. Staff note that three questions are often asked but missing, and two answers are often misunderstood.
questions.question: Which TWO adjustments are most appropriate?

options.A: Ask Claude to draft answers for the three missing questions, using source material staff provide.
options.B: Rewrite the two misunderstood answers with Claude, testing the new wording with a few staff before publishing.
options.C: Ask Claude to add 50 more likely questions, so that the FAQ anticipates everything visitors could possibly ask.
options.D: Keep the misunderstood answers because they are technically accurate.
options.E: Remove the FAQ and return to relying on staff knowledge, since the gaps show the document cannot keep up with visitors' questions.

questions.explanation: Use real-world feedback to make targeted changes: fill observed gaps with grounded content and fix confusing answers, then test the changes.

why_incorrect.C: Adding unrequested questions makes the FAQ harder to use.
why_incorrect.D: If readers misunderstand, the answer fails its purpose.
why_incorrect.E: The FAQ has value; targeted fixes are better than removal.

questions.scenario: Tailspin Travel tried two versions of Project instructions for drafting client itineraries. Version A produces more detailed itineraries; Version B produces shorter ones that agents edit less. Agents prefer B, but two clients complained B omitted transfer times.
questions.question: What is the best decision?

options.A: Switch back to Version A, since its more detailed itineraries are less likely to omit any client-facing information.
options.B: Alternate between A and B each week.
options.C: Keep Version B, add an explicit requirement for transfer times, and confirm with fresh test itineraries.
options.D: Keep Version B unchanged, since agents use it every day and their preference is the best measure of quality.

questions.explanation: Adjust based on evidence from all stakeholders: keep what works, fix the specific failure, and verify the change.

why_incorrect.A: This discards B's benefits; the specific gap can be fixed instead.
why_incorrect.B: Alternating does not fix the omission and makes results inconsistent.
why_incorrect.D: This ignores a client-facing omission.

questions.scenario: After a week of feedback, Trey Research's research assistant Project has accumulated ten new instructions added one at a time. Results are now worse than before.
questions.question: What is the most sensible way to proceed?

options.A: Review the instructions together, remove duplicates and conflicts, and test the result on fixed sample questions.
options.B: Add one more instruction telling Claude to follow all previous instructions carefully and consistently.
options.C: Switch to a different model whenever results get worse, since the newer instructions may suit another model better.
options.D: Revert permanently to having no instructions.

questions.explanation: Feedback-driven changes accumulate. Periodically consolidating instructions and testing against a fixed set of examples keeps them coherent.

why_incorrect.B: Adding more instructions compounds the conflict and clutter.
why_incorrect.C: The cause is the instructions, not the model.
why_incorrect.D: This discards all improvements instead of fixing the accumulated issues.

questions.scenario: Hannah at Margie's Travel re-uploads the same 50-page supplier handbook to a new chat several times a day and is hitting her usage limit.
