questions.scenario: Fabrikam Retail's engineering team stores a long-lived Anthropic API key in a shared `.env` file committed to a private repository so that every service can call the Claude API.
questions.question: Which remediation best closes the authentication gap?

options.A: Revoke and rotate the key, purge it from repository history, and issue per-service credentials from a secrets manager or workload identity federation, scoped by workspace
options.B: Keep the key but restrict repository access to senior engineers
options.C: Base64-encode the key in the `.env` file
options.D: Add a code comment asking developers not to copy the key elsewhere

questions.explanation: Long-lived shared keys in source control are a common credential-exposure path: anyone with repository access, or any leaked clone, can use them, and usage cannot be attributed. Remediation is to revoke and rotate the key, remove it from history, and give each service its own credential from a secrets manager or a short-lived workload identity, scoped to the workspace it needs. Making the repository private or adding a comment does not change exposure.

why_incorrect.B: Fewer readers reduces exposure but leaves a shared, long-lived, unattributable secret in source control.
why_incorrect.C: Encoding is not encryption; the key remains trivially recoverable.
why_incorrect.D: A comment provides no technical control.

questions.scenario: Meridian Clinics' patient-portal assistant uses a `get_lab_results(patient_id)` tool. A penetration test shows that a logged-in patient can ask 'show lab results for patient 10442' and receive another patient's results.
questions.question: What is the root cause and correct fix?

options.A: The system prompt is too permissive; add a rule that patients may only ask about themselves
options.B: The tool trusts a model-supplied identifier; bind the tool to the authenticated session's patient identity on the server and reject mismatched IDs
options.C: The model is hallucinating patient IDs; use a more capable model
options.D: Patient IDs are guessable; switch to random UUIDs

questions.explanation: This is an insecure direct object reference reached through the model: the tool trusts a model-supplied `patient_id`. The fix is to derive the patient identity from the authenticated session on the server side and ignore or reject any identifier the model supplies that does not match, so the model has no way to request another patient's data. Prompt instructions and output filters are bypassable; hiding IDs from users does not stop guessing.

why_incorrect.A: Prompt rules can be bypassed; the backend still serves any ID it is given.
why_incorrect.C: The model is following the user's request; the vulnerability is in the tool's authorisation logic.
why_incorrect.D: Harder-to-guess IDs reduce enumeration but do not enforce that a patient can only see their own data.

questions.scenario: Kestrel Payments' real-time fraud-explanation feature must show an analyst a two-sentence rationale within one second p95. A prototype on Claude Opus 5.5 at `high` effort scores 94% on the rationale-quality eval with 4.2-second p95 latency; at `low` effort it scores 92% with 1.1-second p95. Claude Haiku 5.5 at `low` effort scores 90% with 0.6-second p95. The quality floor is 90%.
questions.question: Which configuration is best justified?

options.A: Claude Opus 5.5 at high effort, because quality matters most for fraud
options.B: Claude Opus 5.5 at low effort, because 1.1 seconds is close enough
options.C: Claude Haiku 5.5 at low effort, because it is the only option that meets the latency SLA while meeting the quality floor, then work on prompt improvements to add quality margin
options.D: Claude Opus 5.5 at max effort with streaming so the first token appears sooner

questions.explanation: When a hard latency SLA and a quality floor both apply, choose the configuration that satisfies both with the best margin, and document the trade-off. Claude Haiku 5.5 at low effort meets the 1-second target and exactly meets the 90% floor; Opus at low effort is still slightly over the latency target. The decision should be recorded with the eval evidence and revisited, for example by improving the prompt to add quality margin on the faster model. Picking the highest-quality option ignores the SLA.

why_incorrect.A: 4.2-second p95 latency breaks the stated one-second requirement.
why_incorrect.B: It misses the agreed SLA; trade-offs should be decided against stated targets, not proximity.
why_incorrect.D: Max effort increases total latency, and analysts need the whole two-sentence rationale.

questions.scenario: Alpine Ski House's booking chatbot feels slow: users wait about six seconds before any text appears, although total answer quality is good.
questions.question: Which TWO changes most directly improve perceived latency without lowering quality? (Choose 2.)

options.A: Cut `max_tokens` to 200 so responses finish sooner
options.B: Stream responses to the UI so text appears as it is generated
options.C: Switch to the smallest model regardless of eval results
options.D: Cache the stable system prompt and tool definitions so repeated requests process less uncached input
options.E: Send the same request twice and use whichever returns first

questions.explanation: Perceived latency is dominated by time to first token. Streaming the response shows text as soon as it is generated, and prompt caching of the stable prefix (system prompt and tools) reduces input processing time on repeated requests. Switching to a smaller model or cutting `max_tokens` can reduce latency but may reduce quality or truncate answers, which the question rules out.

why_incorrect.A: A low cap risks truncated answers, lowering quality.
why_incorrect.C: This may reduce quality, which the requirement says to preserve.
why_incorrect.E: Duplicate requests double cost and consume rate limits for marginal gains.

questions.scenario: Trey Research's analysts ask for 'faster answers' from a Claude Opus 5.5 research agent hosted on Amazon Bedrock. A colleague suggests enabling fast mode.
questions.question: What should the architect point out, as of 2026-10-24?

options.A: Fast mode is free on Bedrock and should be enabled immediately
options.B: Fast mode reduces quality by switching to a smaller model
options.C: Fast mode only works with the Batch API
options.D: Fast mode is not available on Amazon Bedrock; evaluate lower effort, streaming, caching or a faster model for sub-tasks instead, or weigh a platform change explicitly

questions.explanation: Fast mode is a research preview that runs the same model at higher output speed for premium pricing, but as of 2026-10-24 it is available on the Claude API only, not on Amazon Bedrock, Google Cloud or Microsoft Foundry. On Bedrock, the levers are lowering effort for routine requests, streaming, caching and choosing a faster model for sub-tasks, each validated on the eval. Moving platforms for speed alone would also need to account for data-residency and procurement constraints.

why_incorrect.A: Fast mode carries premium pricing and is not offered on Bedrock.
why_incorrect.B: Fast mode runs the same model at higher output speed; the issue here is availability and price.
why_incorrect.C: Fast mode is not available with the Batch API.

questions.scenario: Tailspin Insurance's claims agent occasionally produces wrong settlement recommendations. Each request is logged only as the final answer text and total latency. Engineers cannot reconstruct why a recommendation was made.
questions.question: Which observability design best supports diagnosis at scale?

options.A: Emit a trace per task with spans for every model call and tool call, capturing inputs and outputs (with redaction), stop reason, token usage, latency, and prompt and model version
options.B: Ask the agent to include its full reasoning in the final answer so logs contain the explanation
options.C: Log only failed requests to save storage
options.D: Increase log retention for the existing final-answer logs

questions.explanation: Agentic systems need traces, not just final outputs: a trace ID per task, spans for each model call and tool call with inputs, outputs, `stop_reason`, token usage and latency, plus the prompt and model version used. This lets engineers replay a failure, see which tool returned what, and correlate errors with releases. Sensitive fields should be redacted or tokenised before storage. More verbose final answers or sampling only successes do not reveal the causal chain.

why_incorrect.B: This inflates user-facing output and still omits tool inputs and results needed for diagnosis.
why_incorrect.C: Failures are often detected later; without traces of normal runs you cannot compare or find silent errors.
why_incorrect.D: Keeping more of the same insufficient data does not reveal the causal chain.

questions.scenario: Lucerne Publishing runs Claude Code across 300 developers and wants dashboards showing usage, cost and tool acceptance by team, exported to its existing observability platform.
questions.question: Which approach is supported by Claude Code?

options.A: Ask each developer to paste session summaries into a shared spreadsheet weekly
options.B: Enable Claude Code's OpenTelemetry export through managed settings and send metrics and events to the existing collector
options.C: Parse developers' shell history for `claude` invocations
options.D: Rely only on the monthly invoice total

questions.explanation: Claude Code can export metrics and events through OpenTelemetry when telemetry is enabled (for example `CLAUDE_CODE_ENABLE_TELEMETRY=1` with an OTLP exporter configured). Administrators can deliver these variables, including the exporter selectors, through managed settings so they apply consistently to every developer, then route data to their existing collector. Scraping terminal output or surveying developers does not scale and misses cost data.

why_incorrect.A: Manual reporting is incomplete, delayed and unreliable at 300 users.
why_incorrect.C: Shell history shows invocations, not tokens, cost or tool decisions.
why_incorrect.D: An invoice total cannot be broken down by team, tool use or acceptance rate.

questions.scenario: Contoso Health wants full prompt and response logging for its clinical assistant to support incident investigation. Prompts contain protected health information (PHI).
questions.question: Which TWO practices best balance observability with privacy obligations? (Choose 2.)

options.A: Redact or tokenise PHI in traces at capture time, keeping a controlled re-identification path for authorised investigators
options.B: Disable prompt logging entirely so no PHI is ever stored
options.C: Send full transcripts to the marketing analytics platform so product teams can explore them
options.D: Store any logs that contain PHI in an access-controlled, encrypted, audited store with a defined retention period
options.E: Log everything unredacted but delete it after one hour

questions.explanation: Observability data is itself sensitive data. PHI should be redacted or tokenised at capture time where possible, with re-identification limited to an authorised process. Logs containing PHI must sit in a store with access controls, encryption, audit trails and a retention schedule aligned to policy. Disabling logging leaves incidents uninvestigable, and sending raw transcripts to a general-purpose analytics tool widens exposure.

why_incorrect.B: This removes the ability to investigate incidents and evaluate quality, trading one risk for another.
why_incorrect.C: This widens access to PHI far beyond what is necessary.
why_incorrect.E: Very short retention defeats investigation and unredacted PHI is still exposed while stored.

questions.scenario: Adatum Pharma indexes standard operating procedures (SOPs). Each SOP has numbered sections; a step often says 'as described in 4.2'. Fixed 300-token chunks frequently cut steps in half, and answers miss the referenced section.
questions.question: Which chunking strategy best fits this content?

options.A: Reduce chunk size to 100 tokens so each chunk is more precise
options.B: Index each SOP as a single chunk so nothing is ever cut
options.C: Chunk by section boundaries, attach SOP ID, section number and title as metadata, and allow referenced sections to be fetched by identifier
options.D: Use random overlapping windows so every sentence appears in several chunks

questions.explanation: Chunking should follow the document's natural structure. Splitting at section boundaries keeps steps intact, and attaching metadata such as the SOP ID, section number and title allows the retriever (or a follow-up tool call) to fetch referenced sections like '4.2'. Smaller fixed chunks increase fragmentation, and one chunk per document defeats retrieval precision.

why_incorrect.A: Smaller fixed chunks split steps even more often and lose surrounding context.
why_incorrect.B: Whole-document chunks reduce retrieval precision and push large irrelevant text into context.
why_incorrect.D: Random windows ignore structure and inflate index size without guaranteeing intact steps.

questions.scenario: Woodgrove Bank's policy assistant retrieves chunks such as 'The limit increases to 25% after the review period.' Users complain answers are vague because chunks do not say which product or policy they belong to.
questions.question: Which TWO indexing improvements best address the problem? (Choose 2.)

options.A: Remove chunk overlap to save storage
options.B: Prepend each chunk with a short generated context describing its source document and section before indexing
options.C: Combine embedding search with a lexical index such as BM25 so exact product names and codes are matched
options.D: Increase top-k from 5 to 50 so the right chunk is more likely to be included
options.E: Lower the embedding dimensionality to speed up search

questions.explanation: Chunks lose meaning when separated from their document. Contextual retrieval prepends a short, document-aware description to each chunk before embedding and keyword indexing, which helps both retrievers find the right chunk. Hybrid retrieval combining embeddings with a lexical index (such as BM25) catches exact terms like product codes that embeddings may blur. Reducing overlap or increasing top-k without fixing chunk context mostly adds noise.

why_incorrect.A: Saving storage does not help chunks that lack identifying context.
why_incorrect.D: Retrieving many more chunks adds noise and cost without making individual chunks interpretable.
why_incorrect.E: Speed is not the reported problem, and lower dimensionality can reduce retrieval quality.

questions.scenario: Civic Benefits Agency is building a RAG assistant for caseworkers over a shared vector index containing documents from several departments, some restricted to specific roles.
questions.question: Which indexing design best prevents unauthorised disclosure through retrieval?

options.A: Tell the model in the system prompt not to reveal restricted content
options.B: Redact restricted terms from the model's answer after generation
options.C: Encrypt the embeddings at rest
options.D: Store access-control metadata with every chunk and filter retrieval by the requesting caseworker's verified entitlements before any text reaches the prompt

questions.explanation: In a shared index, access control must be applied at retrieval time, not left to the model. Storing access metadata (department, classification, permitted roles) with each chunk and filtering queries by the caller's verified entitlements ensures restricted text never reaches the prompt. OWASP lists this under vector and embedding weaknesses. Prompt instructions and post-generation redaction are too late: the model has already seen the data.

why_incorrect.A: The restricted text is already in context; prompt instructions are not a reliable control.
why_incorrect.B: Output filtering is incomplete and occurs after the model has processed restricted data.
why_incorrect.C: Encryption at rest protects storage, not which users can retrieve which chunks.

questions.scenario: Fabrikam Retail wants an assistant to answer questions like 'what were total returns for SKU 88-1043 in Q3 by region?' The data lives in a relational warehouse.
questions.question: Which retrieval strategy best matches this data shape and query pattern?

options.A: Provide a read-only, parameterised query tool over a governed warehouse view so Claude can compute the exact aggregation
options.B: Embed every warehouse row as text and use vector search to find relevant rows
options.C: Export the warehouse to PDF reports and use RAG over them
options.D: Put the full quarterly table in the prompt each time

questions.explanation: Aggregations over structured data are answered precisely by querying the database, not by semantic search over text. Giving Claude a tool that runs parameterised, read-only queries against a governed view (or a text-to-SQL step with validation) lets it compute exact totals. Embedding rows as text loses numeric precision and cannot aggregate reliably.

why_incorrect.B: Similarity search cannot reliably aggregate thousands of rows or guarantee exact totals.
why_incorrect.C: This adds staleness and loses the precision of the structured source.
why_incorrect.D: Large tables waste context and invite arithmetic errors when a query could compute the answer.

questions.scenario: Lucerne Publishing's rights team asks questions of two kinds: exact lookups ('which contracts mention clause code RX-14?') and conceptual ones ('which contracts limit audiobook adaptations?'). The current dense-vector retriever does well on the second kind but misses many exact codes.
questions.question: Which retrieval approach best fits both query patterns?

options.A: Replace embeddings with keyword search only
options.B: Hybrid retrieval combining lexical (BM25) and embedding search, with result fusion and reranking
options.C: Increase embedding dimensions until exact codes are matched
options.D: Ask users to tick a box saying whether their query is exact or conceptual

questions.explanation: Exact identifiers and rare tokens are matched well by lexical retrieval such as BM25, while conceptual questions benefit from dense embeddings. Hybrid retrieval runs both and fuses the results, often followed by a reranking step to order the merged set. Abandoning embeddings would hurt conceptual queries, and asking users to choose a mode pushes design complexity to them.

why_incorrect.A: Keyword-only search handles exact codes but loses the conceptual matches the team relies on.
why_incorrect.C: Embedding size does not make dense retrieval reliable for rare exact tokens.
why_incorrect.D: This shifts the routing burden to users and fails for mixed queries.

questions.scenario: Coho Winery's compliance team has a single 180-page regulatory handbook that changes once a year. They ask detailed questions about it several times a day. An engineer proposes building a vector-search pipeline.
questions.question: Which approach is most appropriate?

options.A: Build a vector-search pipeline because RAG is always more accurate than long context
options.B: Fine-tune a model on the handbook so no context is needed
options.C: Place the full handbook in context as a cached prefix and ask questions against it, revisiting RAG only if the corpus grows
options.D: Split the handbook into 180 one-page chunks and send them all in separate requests

questions.explanation: Retrieval is not always required. When the corpus is a single document that fits comfortably in the context window and changes rarely, placing it in context with prompt caching is often simpler and more accurate than chunked retrieval, because the model sees the whole document and cross-references. Caching keeps repeated requests economical. A RAG pipeline becomes worthwhile as the corpus grows beyond what fits or changes frequently.

why_incorrect.A: RAG adds retrieval errors; for one stable document that fits in context, long context is often simpler and more accurate.
why_incorrect.B: Fine-tuning is not the mechanism for document grounding here and loses citation ability.
why_incorrect.D: Separate requests lose cross-references and multiply cost.

questions.scenario: Northwind Lending has an internal credit-bureau API that will be used by its own customer-service application (one backend service), by analysts in Claude Desktop, and by developers in Claude Code.
questions.question: Which integration decisions are most appropriate? (Choose 2.)

options.A: Build an agent-to-agent protocol endpoint so each client negotiates with a 'bureau agent'
options.B: Have each client implement its own bespoke integration for consistency
options.C: Wrap the bureau API in an MCP server so Claude Desktop and Claude Code can both use it through one integration
options.D: Have the customer-service backend call the bureau API directly through a custom tool definition in its own Claude API requests
options.E: Expose the API as a CLI only, and have analysts run commands manually

questions.explanation: MCP standardises how AI applications discover and call tools, so one MCP server can serve many MCP clients such as Claude Desktop and Claude Code without per-client integration work. For a single backend service that the team owns end to end, calling the API directly through a custom tool definition is simpler and avoids an extra hop. Agent-to-agent protocols address coordination between independent agents, which is not the need here.

why_incorrect.A: Agent-to-agent coordination adds complexity when the need is simply to expose a tool.
why_incorrect.B: Bespoke integrations multiply maintenance and are exactly what MCP standardises.
why_incorrect.E: A CLI-only interface does not integrate with Claude Desktop analysts' workflow.

questions.scenario: Wingtip Toys' Claude Code users need to interact with GitHub. The `gh` CLI is installed and authenticated on every developer machine. Someone proposes also installing a GitHub MCP server that exposes 90 tools.
questions.question: What is the strongest argument for preferring the existing CLI in this environment?

options.A: MCP servers are insecure and should never be used for source control
options.B: CLIs are always faster than any API
options.C: Claude Code cannot connect to MCP servers
options.D: The CLI is already authenticated and familiar to the model, and adds no tool definitions to context, whereas 90 MCP tool definitions consume context on every request

questions.explanation: When an agent already has a capable shell and a well-known CLI, the CLI can be the leaner integration: the model is familiar with it, no tool definitions occupy context, and authentication is already handled. MCP shines when clients lack shell access, when you need structured, discoverable tools across many clients, or when you need centrally managed auth. The choice is context-dependent, not a matter of one being universally insecure.

why_incorrect.A: MCP can be deployed securely; this overgeneralises.
why_incorrect.B: Speed depends on the operation; this is not the deciding factor.
why_incorrect.C: Claude Code supports MCP servers.

questions.scenario: Proseware and a logistics partner each run their own autonomous agents. Proseware's procurement agent must negotiate delivery windows with the partner's scheduling agent, which is owned, hosted and secured by the partner.
questions.question: Which integration mechanism best fits this requirement?

options.A: An agent-to-agent integration in which each organisation's agent exchanges task requests and results over an authenticated channel, without exposing internal tools
options.B: Have the partner expose its internal scheduling database as MCP tools that Proseware's agent calls directly
options.C: Share the partner's API credentials with Proseware's agent
options.D: Merge both agents into one shared deployment

questions.explanation: When two independently owned agents need to collaborate on a task, each keeping its own tools, data and policies, an agent-to-agent integration is appropriate: they exchange task requests and results over an authenticated channel without exposing internal tools. Exposing the partner's internal scheduling database as an MCP tool to Proseware's agent would bypass the partner's own controls, and sharing credentials is a security anti-pattern.

why_incorrect.B: This bypasses the partner agent's policies and exposes internal systems across an organisational boundary.
why_incorrect.C: Sharing credentials across organisations removes accountability and violates least privilege.
why_incorrect.D: The agents are owned by different organisations with separate controls; merging them is not realistic or desirable.

questions.scenario: Litware's enterprise agent can handle 40 business procedures, each with several pages of instructions and helper scripts. Loading all of them into the system prompt costs about 90,000 tokens per request and accuracy on routine requests has dropped.
questions.question: Which TWO designs apply progressive discovery effectively? (Choose 2.)

options.A: Package each procedure as an Agent Skill so only names and descriptions load by default and full instructions load when relevant
options.B: Expose procedures as files in a navigable directory with an index the agent can list and read on demand
options.C: Keep all procedures in the system prompt but cache them
options.D: Compress all 40 procedures into a single summary paragraph
options.E: Move to a model with a larger context window

questions.explanation: Progressive discovery (or disclosure) keeps a lightweight index in context and loads detail only when needed. Agent Skills do this by keeping each skill's name and description in context and reading the full instructions and scripts on demand. Similarly, presenting tools or files as a discoverable hierarchy that the agent can list and read when relevant avoids paying for everything up front. Summarising everything into the prompt loses detail, and relying on a larger window keeps the distraction.

why_incorrect.C: Caching reduces price, but the 90,000 tokens still occupy context and dilute attention.
why_incorrect.D: This loses the operational detail the agent needs to execute procedures correctly.
why_incorrect.E: More room does not fix the accuracy loss from irrelevant material.

questions.scenario: An architect at Fourth Coffee is choosing between monolithic context (everything loaded up front) and progressive discovery for a small FAQ assistant with a 3,000-token knowledge base used in every conversation.
questions.question: Which statement best reflects the trade-off?

options.A: Progressive discovery is always better because it minimises tokens
options.B: Monolithic context is reasonable here because the knowledge base is small and almost always relevant; progressive discovery adds round-trips and failure points without enough savings
options.C: Monolithic context is never acceptable in production
options.D: The choice only matters for models with small context windows

questions.explanation: Progressive discovery pays off when the full body of instructions or knowledge is large relative to what any one request needs. For a small knowledge base that is relevant to nearly every conversation, loading it up front is simpler, has no discovery step to fail, and can be cached. The added round-trips and complexity of on-demand loading would not be repaid.

why_incorrect.A: Discovery adds tool calls, latency and a chance of missing content; it is not always better.
why_incorrect.C: Small, always-relevant context is a common and sound production design.
why_incorrect.D: Context quality and cost matter at any window size.

questions.scenario: Relecloud's data agent connects to an MCP server that exposes thousands of operations. Intermediate results (for example 10,000-row query outputs) flow back through the model's context even though the agent only needs a filtered summary.
questions.question: Which approach reduces both tool-definition and intermediate-result overhead?

options.A: Load all tool definitions up front and ask the agent to summarise results itself
options.B: Increase `max_tokens` so large results fit in responses
options.C: Let the agent discover tool interfaces on demand and call them from code in a sandboxed execution environment, returning only filtered results to the model's context
options.D: Paginate results to 10 rows and ask the user to request more

questions.explanation: Having the agent write code that calls tools inside a code-execution environment lets it discover only the tool interfaces it needs and filter or aggregate large intermediate results before anything returns to the model's context. This combines progressive discovery of tools with keeping bulky data out of the context window. Bigger windows or more verbose summaries keep the overhead.

why_incorrect.A: Every definition and every large result still passes through context.
why_incorrect.B: `max_tokens` limits output, not the size of tool results entering context.
why_incorrect.D: This degrades the analysis and pushes work onto the user.

questions.scenario: Northwind Lending is launching a Claude assistant that drafts adverse-action explanations for declined loan applications. The product owner proposes 'user satisfaction' as the single success metric.
questions.question: Which metric set is most appropriate for this use case?

options.A: User satisfaction score only, because the explanation is customer-facing
options.B: BLEU score against a set of previously written letters
options.C: Average output length, to keep letters concise
options.D: Accuracy of stated reasons against the decision record, completeness of required disclosures, a compliance check for prohibited factors, and latency and cost per explanation

questions.explanation: Success criteria should be specific, measurable and cover every dimension that matters for the use case. For regulated adverse-action explanations, that means factual accuracy against the decision record, inclusion of required reasons, safety and compliance checks (for example no prohibited factors mentioned), plus operational measures of latency and cost per explanation. Satisfaction alone cannot detect a compliant-sounding but inaccurate letter.

why_incorrect.A: Satisfaction does not measure accuracy or regulatory completeness.
why_incorrect.B: Surface-overlap metrics reward wording similarity, not correctness or compliance.
why_incorrect.C: Length is at most a secondary style metric and says nothing about correctness.

questions.scenario: Proseware is defining evaluation metrics for an agent that can open pull requests in internal repositories. Functional metrics (task success rate, review acceptance) are already defined.
questions.question: Which TWO additional metrics are most important to track for security? (Choose 2.)

options.A: Attack success rate on a red-team set of injected instructions embedded in issues and files
options.B: Average tokens per pull request
options.C: Rate of attempted out-of-scope actions, such as edits to protected paths or reads of secret files, per hundred tasks
options.D: Percentage of pull requests with a friendly description
options.E: Mean time for reviewers to approve pull requests

questions.explanation: An agent with write capabilities needs security metrics in its evaluation, not just functional ones. Two high-value measures are the rate at which adversarial inputs (for example injected instructions in issues or files) cause the agent to take unintended actions, and the rate of attempted actions outside its allowed scope, such as touching protected paths or secrets. Token usage and response style are useful operationally but do not measure security.

why_incorrect.B: A cost metric, not a security metric.
why_incorrect.D: A style metric that says nothing about security.
why_incorrect.E: Approval speed measures workflow efficiency, not whether the agent behaves safely.

questions.scenario: Bluefin Grocers' dashboard shows cost per request for its recipe assistant fell 30% after a prompt change, and leadership calls the change a success.
questions.question: What additional measure is needed before concluding that the change saved money?

options.A: Cost per successfully completed task, with a quality measure, to check whether users now need more requests to reach a usable result
options.B: The number of cache hits per day
options.C: The model's public benchmark score
options.D: The p99 latency of the new prompt

questions.explanation: Cost per request can fall while total cost rises if users need more requests to get a usable result. The meaningful unit is cost per successfully completed task, paired with a quality measure. If the cheaper prompt causes more follow-up turns or more abandoned sessions, the apparent saving is illusory.

why_incorrect.B: Cache hits are one cost driver, not a measure of whether the overall change saved money.
why_incorrect.C: Benchmarks do not measure this application's task completion.
why_incorrect.D: Latency matters but does not answer whether total cost to complete tasks fell.

questions.scenario: Contoso Health is evaluating a discharge-instructions generator. The team must decide how to measure 'safety' for this use case.
questions.question: Which definition of a safety metric is most actionable?

options.A: Whether the model refuses unsafe requests
options.B: The rate of outputs containing defined clinical harm categories (dosage errors, contradictions of the care plan, omitted red-flag symptoms) on a labelled test set, with zero tolerance for the most severe
options.C: A reviewer's overall impression that outputs 'seem safe'
options.D: The model provider's published safety card

questions.explanation: Actionable safety metrics are operationalised for the specific domain: a defined list of harmful failure categories (for example wrong dosage, contradicting the clinician's plan, omitted red-flag symptoms), a labelled test set covering them, and a target rate with zero tolerance for the most severe categories. Generic statements about 'being safe' or relying on refusals do not tell you whether outputs harm patients.

why_incorrect.A: Refusal behaviour matters but does not measure harm in normal, benign outputs.
why_incorrect.C: Unstructured impressions are not repeatable or comparable across versions.
why_incorrect.D: Provider-level evaluations do not measure this application's domain-specific harms.

questions.scenario: Fabrikam Retail is building an evaluation set for a returns-policy assistant. It has 20,000 historical chat transcripts and a small team of policy experts.
questions.question: Which THREE practices produce a strong evaluation dataset? (Choose 3.)

options.A: Sample real transcripts stratified by topic so the set reflects production traffic
options.B: Use only the 200 most recent transcripts because they are most relevant
options.C: Add expert-written edge cases, such as policy exceptions and adversarial requests, that are rare in history
options.D: Keep a held-out test split that is never used while iterating on prompts
options.E: Have the model under test write the reference answers without expert review

questions.explanation: Good eval sets reflect the real distribution of tasks while deliberately covering edge cases, are labelled reliably, and stay separate from material used to tune prompts. Sampling from real transcripts (stratified by topic), adding expert-written edge cases such as policy exceptions and adversarial inputs, and holding out a test split that is not used during prompt iteration all serve those goals. Using only the easiest or most recent cases biases results, and letting the model under test label its own answers without validation creates circularity.

why_incorrect.B: Recency alone under-represents seasonal and rare cases.
why_incorrect.E: This makes the evaluation circular; errors in references go undetected.

questions.scenario: Lucerne Publishing evaluates a book-blurb generator. Some criteria are objective (length limit, no spoilers of the ending, required ISBN format) and others are subjective (tone fits the genre).
questions.question: Which mixed-method grading approach is most appropriate?

options.A: Human review of every blurb for every criterion
options.B: An LLM judge for every criterion, including length and ISBN format
options.C: Code-based checks for length and ISBN format, an LLM judge with a rubric for spoilers and tone calibrated against human labels, and periodic human audits of a sample
options.D: Only code-based checks, because subjective criteria cannot be evaluated

questions.explanation: Choose the cheapest reliable grader for each criterion. Objective, rule-like checks such as length and format are best handled by code. Criteria like spoiler detection and tone fit can be graded by an LLM judge with a clear rubric, calibrated against a sample of human labels. Humans then audit a slice periodically and handle disagreements. Using humans for everything does not scale, and using an LLM judge for deterministic checks adds cost and variance.

why_incorrect.A: Accurate but slow and costly; it does not scale to regression testing.
why_incorrect.B: Deterministic checks are cheaper and more reliable in code.
why_incorrect.D: Rubric-based LLM grading and human review can evaluate subjective criteria.

questions.scenario: Kestrel Payments' prompt team reports eval accuracy rising from 84% to 97% over six weeks of iteration. After release, production accuracy measured by analyst corrections is about 85%.
questions.question: What is the most likely explanation?

options.A: The model was silently downgraded after release
options.B: Prompt caching serves stale answers in production
options.C: Analysts are correcting answers that were actually right
options.D: The prompts were tuned against the same eval cases until they overfit; the eval lacked a held-out split representative of production traffic

questions.explanation: When eval scores climb steadily during iteration but production does not move, the usual cause is overfitting to the eval: the team has tuned prompts against the same cases repeatedly, possibly adding examples drawn from them. A held-out test split, refreshed with recent production samples, gives an honest estimate. Model drift or caching would not explain a consistent gap between the eval set and production.

why_incorrect.A: Model versions are pinned by ID; the pattern points to evaluation design.
why_incorrect.B: Caching reuses input processing, not answers; it does not change outputs.
why_incorrect.C: Possible in a few cases, but it would not explain a consistent 12-point gap.

questions.scenario: Tailspin Insurance plans to use Claude Sonnet 5.5 as an LLM judge to grade claim-summary quality on a 1–5 scale. Early results show the judge rarely gives scores below 4.
questions.question: Which TWO steps most improve the judge's reliability? (Choose 2.)

options.A: Remove the rubric so the judge uses its own judgement
options.B: Replace the vague 1–5 scale with a rubric that defines concrete criteria for each level, or binary pass/fail per criterion
options.C: Use the same system prompt for the judge as for the summary generator
options.D: Measure agreement between the judge and a sample of human-labelled summaries and refine the rubric until agreement is acceptable
options.E: Average the judge's score with the summary length to break ties

questions.explanation: LLM judges need a precise rubric with concrete descriptions of each score level (or a binary pass/fail per criterion), and they need calibration against human labels to measure agreement. Asking the judge to reason before scoring and grading one criterion at a time also helps. Removing the rubric, or using the same prompt as the generator, makes scores less reliable.

why_incorrect.A: Without criteria, scores become inconsistent and drift toward leniency.
why_incorrect.C: Sharing the generator's prompt biases the judge toward the generator's own framing.
why_incorrect.E: Length is unrelated to quality and adds noise.

questions.scenario: Fabrikam Retail wants to A/B test a new system prompt for its live shopping assistant. The primary metric is the add-to-cart rate after an assistant interaction.
questions.question: Which TWO design choices are most important for a valid test? (Choose 2.)

options.A: Randomise assignment at the user or session level so each user consistently sees one variant
options.B: Change the model and the prompt together to maximise the chance of a visible effect
options.C: Alternate variants on every message within a conversation
options.D: Pre-register the primary metric and required sample size from a power calculation, and do not stop early on a promising interim result
options.E: Stop the test as soon as the new prompt is ahead on a daily dashboard

questions.explanation: Valid A/B tests randomise at the right unit (usually the user or session, so one person does not see both variants), fix the primary metric and sample size in advance from a power calculation, and run until that size is reached rather than stopping when results look good. Changing several things at once or switching variants mid-session confounds the results.

why_incorrect.B: Changing two variables at once makes it impossible to attribute the effect.
why_incorrect.C: Within-conversation switching contaminates both variants and confuses users.
why_incorrect.E: Peeking and stopping early inflates false positives.

questions.scenario: Coho Winery's team iterates on a tasting-note generator. Each week they change several prompt sections at once, and quality sometimes improves and sometimes regresses without anyone knowing why.
questions.question: Which iteration practice would most improve their process?

options.A: Version-control prompts, change one element at a time, run the same eval suite on each change, and keep or revert based on the results
options.B: Make bigger changes less often so there are fewer experiments to track
options.C: Judge each change by reading three outputs the author picks
options.D: Let the model rewrite its own prompt each week

questions.explanation: Effective iteration changes one thing at a time, runs the full offline eval suite on each change, records the result against a version-controlled prompt, and keeps or reverts based on evidence. This makes improvements attributable and regressions reversible. Larger batches of changes or decisions based on a few hand-picked examples hide cause and effect.

why_incorrect.B: Bundling changes makes cause and effect even harder to identify.
why_incorrect.C: Hand-picked samples are biased and too small to detect regressions.
why_incorrect.D: Unreviewed self-modification removes control and traceability.

questions.scenario: Relecloud wants to compare Claude Opus 5.5 at `medium` effort with the same model at `low` effort for its ticket-triage agent. Each eval run costs real money and takes an hour.
questions.question: Which experiment design gives a trustworthy answer at reasonable cost?

options.A: Run each configuration on a different random sample of 20 cases to save money
options.B: Run both effort levels on the same representative eval set (a paired comparison), compare quality, latency and cost per completed task, and apply a decision rule agreed in advance
options.C: Compare one hand-picked difficult case on each configuration
options.D: Compare `low` effort on Claude Haiku 5.5 with `medium` effort on Claude Opus 5.5 to test two ideas at once

questions.explanation: A paired comparison on the same representative eval cases isolates the effect of the single changed variable (effort) and needs fewer cases than unpaired comparisons. Tracking quality, latency and cost per completed task gives the full trade-off, and agreeing the decision rule in advance avoids rationalising results. A small online test first or a single-case comparison would not be trustworthy, and comparing different models at once confounds the result.

why_incorrect.A: Different small samples add noise that can swamp the real difference.
why_incorrect.C: A single case cannot support a decision.
why_incorrect.D: Changing model and effort together confounds the result.

questions.scenario: Wingtip Toys ran an online A/B test of two prompts for 48 hours. Variant B's satisfaction score was 2 points higher with a p-value of 0.04, but traffic during the test was mostly a weekend holiday sale.
questions.question: What is the most appropriate interpretation?

options.A: Roll out variant B immediately because p < 0.05
options.B: Discard variant B because two points is too small to matter
options.C: Treat the result as provisional, because the sample was unrepresentative; extend or rerun the test across typical traffic before full rollout
options.D: Rerun the test with a different metric until one is significant

questions.explanation: A statistically significant result can still fail to generalise if the sample is unrepresentative. A short test dominated by atypical holiday-sale traffic may not reflect normal usage, so the result should be confirmed over a period that covers typical traffic (or analysed by segment) before rollout. Statistical significance alone does not guarantee practical or general validity.

why_incorrect.A: Significance on an unrepresentative sample does not establish that the effect generalises.
why_incorrect.B: Small effects can matter at scale; the issue is representativeness, not size alone.
why_incorrect.D: Searching for a significant metric inflates false positives.

questions.scenario: Meridian Clinics' referral-letter assistant sometimes cites specialist clinics that do not exist. The prompt includes a directory of 400 clinics, and errors cluster on letters for rare specialties.
questions.question: Which TWO interventions most directly address this hallucination pattern? (Choose 2.)

options.A: Add examples of well-written letters for common specialties
options.B: Instruct the assistant to state when no listed clinic matches the specialty, rather than inventing one
options.C: Require the clinic to be selected by ID from the directory, via a lookup tool or schema constraint, and validate the ID before the letter is sent
options.D: Ask the model to sound more confident in its recommendations
options.E: Remove the directory to shorten the prompt

questions.explanation: Fabricated entities near the edge of the provided data usually mean the model is filling gaps instead of admitting none match. Two direct fixes: give the model explicit permission and a defined way to say no matching clinic was found, and constrain the output so the clinic must be chosen from the directory (for example a schema enum or a lookup tool returning valid IDs), then validate it. Making the prompt more creative or adding unrelated examples does not address the gap.

why_incorrect.A: Examples for common specialties do not cover the rare cases where errors occur.
why_incorrect.D: Encouraging confidence increases fabrication risk.
why_incorrect.E: Without the directory the model has no grounding at all.

questions.scenario: Margie's Travel's visa-advice assistant performs well in English but poorly on questions asked in Portuguese. The eval set contains only English cases.
questions.question: What is the best first diagnostic step?

options.A: Switch to the largest model, which should handle all languages better
options.B: Translate all Portuguese questions to English before sending them
options.C: Conclude that Claude does not support Portuguese
options.D: Add Portuguese cases mirroring the English eval and measure which stage fails (retrieval, reasoning or output) on that slice

questions.explanation: Before changing prompts or models, extend the evaluation to cover the failing slice: build a Portuguese test set with the same scenarios and measure where performance drops (retrieval of Portuguese sources, reasoning, or output language). Diagnosis needs data on the failing segment. Switching models or translating everything without evidence may fix the wrong thing.

why_incorrect.A: This may help but is unverified and expensive; without a Portuguese eval you cannot confirm it.
why_incorrect.B: This could help but is a fix chosen without diagnosis and may lose nuance.
why_incorrect.C: Claude is multilingual; the issue needs to be measured, not assumed.

questions.scenario: Trey Research's contract-analysis prompt worked well on an older model. After migrating to a current model, outputs are longer, the model asks clarifying questions the old one never asked, and one rule ('ALWAYS list every clause') causes very long lists of trivial clauses.
questions.question: Which diagnosis best explains these symptoms?

options.A: The prompt is tuned for the old model; the new model follows instructions more literally, so dated absolute rules over-trigger and verbosity defaults differ. Revise the prompt for the new model and re-evaluate
options.B: The new model is less capable and should be rolled back
options.C: The context window is too small for the contracts
options.D: Prompt caching is returning outputs from the old model

questions.explanation: These are signs of model mismatch: the prompt was tuned for an older model's behaviour. Newer models follow instructions more precisely, so absolute rules written to overcome weaker adherence now over-trigger, and they may be calibrated differently on verbosity and clarification. The fix is to revisit the prompt for the new model, removing dated emphasis, stating what 'relevant' means and specifying the desired length and when to ask questions, then re-running the eval.

why_incorrect.B: The symptoms point to prompt-model mismatch, not lower capability.
why_incorrect.C: A small window would cause truncation or errors, not longer outputs and over-applied rules.
why_incorrect.D: Caches are model-scoped and store input processing, not outputs.

questions.scenario: An architect at Alpine Ski House is triaging a list of assistant failures and wants to classify each by root cause before choosing fixes.
questions.question: Which pairing of symptom and most likely root cause is correct?

options.A: A response ends mid-sentence: a rate-limit problem
options.B: An answer contradicts a policy document present in the context: a grounding or prompt-structure problem
options.C: The model picks the wrong one of two near-identical tools: a caching problem
options.D: JSON output occasionally fails to parse: a context-window problem

questions.explanation: Matching symptoms to causes guides the fix. An answer that contradicts a document present in the context points to a prompt or grounding problem (for example the document is buried or the instructions do not prioritise it). Truncated output points to `max_tokens`, malformed JSON points to missing structured-output constraints, and wrong tool choice between overlapping tools points to tool design. Attributing these to rate limits or caching is a mismatch.

why_incorrect.A: Truncation mid-sentence is typically `max_tokens`; rate limits return errors.
why_incorrect.C: This points to overlapping tool design, not caching.
why_incorrect.D: Parsing failures point to missing format constraints such as structured outputs.

questions.scenario: Fabrikam Retail runs a nightly job that generates 80,000 personalised email drafts using a shared 6,000-token brand guide followed by per-customer data. Nobody reads the drafts until the next morning.
questions.question: Which TWO optimisations most reduce cost without affecting quality? (Choose 2.)

options.A: Set `max_tokens` to 100 to cap output cost
options.B: Switch to the smallest model without evaluating draft quality
options.C: Submit the job through the Message Batches API
options.D: Put the shared brand guide first with a cache breakpoint and the per-customer data after it
options.E: Generate drafts synchronously during business hours to reduce queueing

questions.explanation: For latency-insensitive bulk jobs, the Message Batches API processes requests asynchronously at a discount. Placing the shared brand guide first with a cache breakpoint lets requests reuse the cached prefix, reducing input cost further, while per-customer data follows the breakpoint. Shrinking `max_tokens` risks truncation, and switching models without evaluation risks quality.

why_incorrect.A: A tight cap risks truncated drafts, which affects quality.
why_incorrect.B: An unevaluated model change risks quality, which the requirement excludes.
why_incorrect.E: Synchronous processing forgoes the batch discount and gives no benefit for an overnight job.

questions.scenario: Kestrel Payments switches effort between `low` and `high` on alternate turns of a long agent conversation to save money. Afterwards, cache reads on the conversation history drop sharply and costs rise.
questions.question: What explains the cost increase, and what is a better approach?

options.A: Low effort produces longer outputs, which increases cost
options.B: Caching only works at `high` effort
options.C: Changing top-level effort between requests invalidates the cached message history; pin effort per route, or use the per-message effort mechanism where supported
options.D: Switch to a different model on low-effort turns instead

questions.explanation: Thinking and effort settings are part of what the cache keys on, so changing the top-level effort between requests invalidates the cached message history. Pin effort per route instead, or, on models that support it, use the per-message effort mechanism, which changes effort without that invalidation (a beta feature as of 2026-10-24). Switching models would also break the cache, because caches are model-scoped.

why_incorrect.A: Lower effort generally reduces output tokens; the cost rise comes from cache invalidation.
why_incorrect.B: Caching works at any effort level; changing the level between requests is the problem.
why_incorrect.D: Caches are model-scoped, so alternating models also discards the cached history.

questions.scenario: Litware's document-QA service shows p95 latency of 9 seconds. Profiling shows 70% of time is input processing of a large, unchanging instruction and reference block, and 30% is output generation of short answers.
questions.question: Which optimisation targets the dominant latency component?

options.A: Ask for shorter answers to cut output time
options.B: Increase `max_tokens` to avoid truncation retries
options.C: Split the reference block across parallel requests and merge answers
options.D: Cache the unchanging instruction and reference block so repeated requests skip reprocessing it

questions.explanation: Optimise the dominant stage first. When most latency comes from processing a large, unchanging input prefix, prompt caching reduces time to first token on cache hits as well as cost. Output-side measures (shorter answers, faster output speed) would address only 30% of the time. Splitting the reference block across parallel requests would lose shared context.

why_incorrect.A: Output is only 30% of latency; this leaves the dominant input-processing cost untouched.
why_incorrect.B: There is no evidence of truncation; this does not reduce input processing.
why_incorrect.C: Parallel fragments lose shared context and multiply requests.

questions.scenario: Northwind Lending is moving a document-classification service to production. Leadership wants early warning if quality degrades, for example after input formats change.
questions.question: Which TWO monitoring practices provide the best early warning of quality degradation? (Choose 2.)

options.A: Continuously score a sample of live traffic with automated checks or an LLM judge, calibrated by periodic human review
options.B: Alert on drift in input and output distributions, such as document types, label proportions and stop-reason rates
options.C: Monitor API uptime only
options.D: Review the monthly invoice for unusual totals
options.E: Re-run the offline eval once a year

questions.explanation: Quality monitoring in production needs both a direct and an indirect signal. Running an LLM judge or rule checks on a sampled slice of live traffic, with periodic human review to keep the judge honest, measures quality directly. Tracking input and output distribution drift (document types, lengths, label proportions, refusal and `max_tokens` stop rates) gives early indicators even before quality labels arrive. Uptime and invoice totals do not detect quality changes.

why_incorrect.C: Uptime shows availability, not whether outputs are correct.
why_incorrect.D: Cost totals are lagging and say little about quality.
why_incorrect.E: Annual checks are far too infrequent for early warning.

questions.scenario: Tailspin Insurance's dashboards show a sudden rise in HTTP 429 responses from the Claude API every weekday at 09:00 when batch-style back-office jobs start alongside interactive traffic.
questions.question: Which response best addresses the problem?

options.A: Attribute usage by workload, move back-office jobs to the Batch API or off-peak scheduling, and use backoff that honours `retry-after` for interactive retries
options.B: Retry every 429 immediately in a tight loop until it succeeds
options.C: Switch all traffic to a larger model to get higher limits
options.D: Ignore 429s because the SDK retries automatically

questions.explanation: 429 responses indicate rate limits are being exceeded. Monitoring should break usage down by workload so the cause is visible, and the fix is to separate and shape traffic: move back-office jobs to the Batch API or schedule them off-peak, honour `retry-after` with exponential backoff, and request higher limits if sustained demand justifies it. Retrying immediately makes contention worse.

why_incorrect.B: Immediate retries add load and prolong throttling.
why_incorrect.C: Limits are not increased by switching to a larger model, and costs would rise.
why_incorrect.D: SDK retries help transient spikes but do not resolve systematic contention between workloads.

questions.scenario: Woodgrove Bank wants its monitoring to detect possible prompt-injection or data-exfiltration attempts against its customer-facing assistant.
questions.question: Which monitoring signal is most useful for this purpose?

options.A: Total daily token usage
options.B: Alerts on anomalous tool-use behaviour, such as unusual data-access sequences, bulk record retrieval or calls to unapproved destinations, correlated by session
options.C: Average response latency
options.D: The count of refusals only

questions.explanation: Security monitoring for LLM applications should look at behaviour, not only at volumes. Alerting on anomalous tool-use patterns, such as unusual sequences of data-access tools, bulk retrieval of records, or attempts to reach unapproved destinations, catches injection and exfiltration attempts that have bypassed prompt-level defences. Aggregate token counts or latency are too coarse and refusals are only a partial signal.

why_incorrect.A: Aggregate tokens are too coarse to identify a specific attack.
why_incorrect.C: Latency changes are not a reliable indicator of injection or exfiltration.
why_incorrect.D: Successful attacks often do not trigger refusals, so this misses the most important cases.

questions.scenario: Kestrel Payments is designing guardrails for a merchant-support assistant that can look up transactions and issue small goodwill credits up to a fixed limit.
questions.question: Which THREE controls form a sound layered guardrail design? (Choose 3.)

options.A: Screen inputs with a lightweight classifier for abuse and injection patterns before the main model call
options.B: Enforce credit caps and daily per-merchant totals in the credit tool's backend, independent of the model
options.C: Scan outputs for sensitive data such as full card numbers before they reach the user
options.D: Rely on a system-prompt rule that the assistant must never exceed the credit limit
options.E: Let the model decide when a credit is justified with no further checks, because it has good judgement

questions.explanation: Effective guardrails are layered and the strongest ones are deterministic. Input screening (for example a fast classifier for abuse or injection patterns) reduces risk early. Hard limits enforced in the credit tool's backend (amount caps, per-merchant daily totals) hold regardless of what the model says. Output checks for sensitive data such as full card numbers stop leakage. Relying on the system prompt or a single model's judgement alone is not a guardrail architecture.

why_incorrect.D: A prompt rule is guidance, not enforcement; the backend must enforce limits.
why_incorrect.E: Unchecked model discretion over money is the excessive-agency risk guardrails exist to contain.

questions.scenario: Fourth Coffee's public chatbot occasionally gets attempts to make it write abusive content about competitors. The team wants a cheap pre-screen before the main model runs.
questions.question: Which design is most appropriate?

options.A: A static keyword blocklist only
options.B: Generate the response first and screen only the output
options.C: A fast, low-cost model call that classifies each input against a defined policy and returns a structured verdict, with flagged inputs routed to a safe fallback
options.D: Ask users to agree to terms of use before chatting

questions.explanation: A common harmlessness-screening pattern is a fast, low-cost model call that classifies user input against a defined policy and returns a structured verdict, with flagged inputs routed to a safe response or review. It runs before the main model, adds little latency and can be tuned and evaluated independently. Blocklists alone are easy to evade, and screening only after generation wastes cost and risks exposure.

why_incorrect.A: Keyword lists are easily evaded and generate false positives.
why_incorrect.B: Output screening is useful as a second layer, but without input screening every abusive prompt incurs the main model's cost.
why_incorrect.D: Terms set expectations but do not technically prevent abuse.

questions.scenario: Proseware's coding agent runs shell commands in CI. A security review asks how to prevent it from exfiltrating secrets to arbitrary internet hosts if it is manipulated by malicious content in a dependency's README.
questions.question: Which guardrail is most effective?

options.A: Add a prompt instruction not to send secrets anywhere
options.B: Review CI logs weekly for suspicious outbound requests
options.C: Use a more capable model so it recognises malicious README content
options.D: Run the agent in a sandbox with egress restricted to an allowlist of required hosts and with only the minimum secrets available

questions.explanation: Network and filesystem isolation enforced by the environment is a hard boundary that holds even if the agent is manipulated. Running the agent in a sandbox whose egress is restricted to an allowlist of required hosts, with no secrets mounted beyond those strictly needed, prevents exfiltration regardless of the model's behaviour. Prompt warnings and post-hoc log review do not prevent the action.

why_incorrect.A: Instructions can be overridden by injected content; they do not block network access.
why_incorrect.B: Detection after the fact does not prevent the exfiltration.
why_incorrect.C: Capability helps but is not a guaranteed boundary.

questions.scenario: Civic Benefits Agency's guardrail classifier blocks 6% of legitimate questions about domestic-violence support services, frustrating vulnerable users.
questions.question: What is the best response?

options.A: Add legitimate sensitive-topic queries to the guardrail eval, refine the policy with allowed and disallowed examples, and route borderline cases to a helpful safe response instead of a hard block
options.B: Remove the guardrail entirely
options.C: Accept the false positives as the cost of safety
options.D: Add 'domestic violence' to an allowlist that bypasses all checks

questions.explanation: Guardrails have false positives as well as false negatives, and both need measurement. The team should build an evaluation set that includes legitimate sensitive-topic queries, tune the policy and classifier prompt with examples of allowed versus disallowed requests, and route borderline cases to a safe, helpful response (for example signposting support services) rather than a hard block. Removing the guardrail or accepting the harm to users are both poor trade-offs.

why_incorrect.B: This removes protection against genuinely harmful requests.
why_incorrect.C: Blocking vulnerable users from support information is itself a harm that should be reduced.
why_incorrect.D: A blanket bypass can be abused by attackers who include the phrase.

questions.scenario: Adatum Pharma's research agent can browse the web, read internal documents and send email. A threat-modelling workshop is identifying the most serious failure mode.
questions.question: Which risk combination is most serious and why?

options.A: Occasional hallucinated citations in research summaries
options.B: Untrusted web content, access to internal documents and the ability to email externally together enable injection-driven data exfiltration
options.C: Higher token cost from browsing
options.D: Slow responses when many documents are read

questions.explanation: The most dangerous combination in agentic systems is access to private data, exposure to untrusted content and the ability to communicate externally. Together they allow an indirect prompt injection in a web page to instruct the agent to read internal documents and email them out. Breaking any leg of that combination, for example by removing external email or isolating untrusted content from private data access, sharply reduces risk.

why_incorrect.A: A real quality risk, but far less severe than data exfiltration.
why_incorrect.C: Cost is an operational concern, not the most serious security failure mode.
why_incorrect.D: Latency affects user experience, not security.

questions.scenario: A product manager at Wingtip Toys says 'Claude is deterministic if we use the same prompt, so we can skip regression testing after we change unrelated code'.
questions.question: Which TWO statements correct this misunderstanding? (Choose 2.)

options.A: Outputs can vary between runs with identical inputs, so quality should be measured statistically over a test set rather than by exact matching
options.B: Setting `temperature` to 0 makes current models fully deterministic
options.C: Changes to surrounding code such as retrieval or templates change the model's inputs, so regression evaluation is still needed
options.D: Prompt caching guarantees identical outputs for identical prompts
options.E: Determinism only matters for code generation

questions.explanation: LLM outputs can vary between runs even with the same input, and current models do not accept sampling parameters such as `temperature` to force determinism. Systems should therefore be evaluated statistically over a test set rather than by exact output matching. Separately, changes to surrounding code (retrieval, tool results, templates) change what the model sees, so regression tests remain necessary.

why_incorrect.B: Sampling parameters are not accepted on current models.
why_incorrect.D: Caching reuses input processing; it does not cache or fix outputs.
why_incorrect.E: Variability affects all outputs and how they should be evaluated.

questions.scenario: Tailspin Insurance's claims agent runs unattended overnight. One night it loops on a failing tool for six hours, consuming a large share of the monthly budget.
questions.question: Which TWO controls address this failure mode? (Choose 2.)

options.A: Use a more capable model so it notices it is looping
options.B: Enforce per-task caps on iterations, elapsed time and spend outside the model, with alerting on abnormal usage
options.C: Increase the context window so the agent remembers earlier failures
options.D: Return explicit error results from failing tools and define when the agent should stop and escalate
options.E: Run the agent only during business hours

questions.explanation: Unbounded consumption is a recognised LLM risk. Agents need hard limits on iterations, wall-clock time and spend per task, enforced outside the model, plus alerting when usage deviates from normal. Tools should return clear error results so the agent can stop or escalate rather than retry blindly. More capable models or longer context do not prevent runaway loops.

why_incorrect.A: Capability may help but provides no guaranteed bound on spend.
why_incorrect.C: More memory does not cap consumption.
why_incorrect.E: Runaway loops can happen at any time; limits are needed regardless of schedule.

questions.scenario: Lucerne Publishing's summarisation tool sometimes produces summaries of long manuscripts that omit the final chapters, while still reading confidently.
questions.question: Which limitation is most likely at play, and how should it be mitigated?

options.A: The model refuses to summarise final chapters for safety reasons
options.B: Prompt caching drops the end of long documents
options.C: Uneven coverage of very long inputs (or silent truncation upstream); verify the full text is sent, then summarise per chapter and merge so coverage can be checked
options.D: The model needs a `temperature` adjustment to read further

questions.explanation: Long-input tasks can suffer from uneven attention or from inputs that exceed what was actually sent (for example, the pipeline silently truncating to fit). The first check is whether the full manuscript reached the model; then decompose summarisation by chapter and merge, which gives each section full attention and makes omissions detectable. A confident tone is not evidence of completeness.

why_incorrect.A: There is no refusal signal; the output is a confident but incomplete summary.
why_incorrect.B: Caching does not drop content from requests.
why_incorrect.D: Sampling parameters do not affect how much input is read and are not accepted on current models.

questions.scenario: Woodgrove Bank's operations agent prepares wire-transfer corrections. Regulators expect a human to approve each correction, and analysts complain that approval screens show only 'Approve correction?'.
questions.question: Which human-in-the-loop design is most effective?

options.A: Batch corrections and let analysts approve 50 at once to save time
options.B: Skip human approval when the model's confidence exceeds 95%
options.C: Let the agent execute and notify analysts afterwards
options.D: Show the exact proposed action, the evidence and policy rule used, and any uncertainty; run deterministic validation first; and record each approver's decision and rationale for audit

questions.explanation: Approval is only meaningful if the reviewer has what they need to decide. The approval step should present the exact action (accounts, amounts, before and after), the evidence the agent used, the policy rule applied and any uncertainty, and should record the approver's decision for audit. Deterministic validation runs before the human sees it. Approving in bulk or relying on the model's confidence undermines oversight.

why_incorrect.A: Bulk approval encourages rubber-stamping and weakens oversight.
why_incorrect.B: Model confidence is not calibrated authority and regulators expect human approval for each correction.
why_incorrect.C: Post-hoc notification is not approval.

questions.scenario: Meridian Clinics uses Claude to draft responses to patient portal messages. Clinical staff review every draft, but review time is now the bottleneck.
questions.question: Which approach best reduces review burden without weakening oversight of risky messages?

options.A: Tier review by risk: clinicians fully review drafts about symptoms or medications, while low-risk administrative replies get lighter review or sampling, with monitoring of the risk classifier
options.B: Remove review for all messages once accuracy exceeds 90% on the eval
options.C: Review a random 10% of all drafts regardless of content
options.D: Have Claude review its own drafts instead of clinicians

questions.explanation: Risk-based review focuses human attention where it matters. Classify messages by risk (for example clinical symptoms versus appointment logistics), require full clinician review of high-risk categories, and allow lighter review or sampling for low-risk administrative messages, with monitoring to verify the classification. Removing review entirely or reviewing randomly ignores risk.

why_incorrect.B: Aggregate accuracy hides rare, high-severity errors in clinical messages.
why_incorrect.C: Random sampling gives high-risk messages the same light oversight as routine ones.
why_incorrect.D: Self-review is not independent oversight for clinical content.

questions.scenario: Northwind Lending added human approval to an agent's account-closure tool. Audits show approvers accept 99.7% of requests and median review time is four seconds.
questions.question: Which TWO actions best address this automation-bias risk? (Choose 2.)

options.A: Require approvers to confirm the specific facts that justify closure, shown alongside the evidence, rather than a single approve button
options.B: Remove the approval step because approvers add no value
options.C: Require three approvers instead of one
options.D: Seed the approval queue with known-incorrect requests and measure reviewer catch rates
options.E: Show approvers the model's confidence score in large text

questions.explanation: Very high acceptance with very short review times suggests rubber-stamping. Countermeasures include presenting the evidence and requiring approvers to confirm specific facts (not just click approve), inserting known-bad test cases to measure whether reviewers catch them, and tracking reviewer accuracy. Simply adding more approvers or removing the step does not restore meaningful oversight.

why_incorrect.B: Removing oversight for an irreversible action increases risk; the step needs to be made effective.
why_incorrect.C: More approvers can each rubber-stamp; it multiplies cost without fixing the behaviour.
why_incorrect.E: Highlighting model confidence tends to increase automation bias.

questions.scenario: An architect at Alpine Ski House is deciding which agent actions in a booking system should require human confirmation.
questions.question: Which principle should guide the decision?

options.A: Require confirmation for every tool call so nothing happens without a human
options.B: Require confirmation based on reversibility and impact: irreversible, high-value or externally visible actions need approval, while read-only and easily reversible actions proceed with logging
options.C: Require confirmation only when the model asks for it
options.D: Require confirmation only for actions taken outside business hours

questions.explanation: Human-in-the-loop effort should scale with the consequences of an action: irreversible, high-impact or externally visible actions (refunds above a threshold, cancellations affecting other guests, messages to many customers) need confirmation, while read-only or easily reversible actions can proceed automatically with logging. Requiring confirmation for everything creates fatigue; requiring it for nothing removes oversight.

why_incorrect.A: Confirming everything causes approval fatigue and erodes attention for the actions that matter.
why_incorrect.C: The model should not decide which of its own actions need oversight.
why_incorrect.D: Time of day is unrelated to the consequence of an action.

questions.scenario: Contoso Health is planning a Claude-based clinical documentation assistant in the United States that will process protected health information (PHI).
questions.question: Which TWO steps are prerequisites from a HIPAA perspective? (Choose 2.)

options.A: Rely on the model's built-in safety training to protect PHI
options.B: Execute a Business Associate Agreement with the provider that covers the specific services and features to be used
options.C: Design for minimum-necessary PHI, with access controls, audit logging and encryption across the data flow
options.D: Add a system-prompt line stating that the assistant is HIPAA compliant
options.E: Use the most capable model, since compliance requires accuracy

questions.explanation: Under HIPAA, a covered entity sending PHI to a vendor needs a Business Associate Agreement (BAA) covering the specific services used, and the architecture must apply the minimum-necessary principle along with administrative, physical and technical safeguards (access control, audit logging, encryption). Model capability, prompt wording or anonymity claims do not substitute for the contractual and technical requirements. Confirm current eligibility of specific features with the provider, as of the date of design.

why_incorrect.A: Model behaviour is not a HIPAA safeguard or a contractual protection.
why_incorrect.D: Compliance is a property of contracts, controls and processes, not a prompt statement.
why_incorrect.E: Accuracy matters clinically but is not a HIPAA prerequisite.

questions.scenario: Fabrikam Retail operates in the EU and wants Claude to personalise marketing emails using customer purchase history. The DPO asks for GDPR-aligned design.
questions.question: Which design choice best reflects GDPR principles?

options.A: Send full customer profiles so the model can find the best personalisation angle
options.B: Hash customer names and send everything else unchanged
options.C: Send only the minimum attributes needed for personalisation, document the lawful basis and processor terms, and suppress customers who have objected to direct marketing
options.D: Avoid documenting the processing so there is less to audit

questions.explanation: GDPR requires a lawful basis for processing, purpose limitation and data minimisation, among other principles. The design should send only the attributes needed for personalisation (for example product categories rather than full order history with addresses), document the lawful basis and processor arrangements, and honour objections to direct marketing. Sending everything 'in case it is useful' violates minimisation.

why_incorrect.A: This conflicts with data minimisation and purpose limitation.
why_incorrect.B: Hashing one field does not make the rest of the personal data compliant or minimal.
why_incorrect.D: GDPR requires accountability and records of processing.

questions.scenario: Civic Benefits Agency is a US government body that requires FedRAMP-authorised cloud services for production systems handling citizen data. A team has prototyped on the Claude API directly.
questions.question: What should the architect do before production?

options.A: Proceed, because the prototype has no security incidents
options.B: Encrypt prompts client-side so the service never sees plain text
options.C: Ask the vendor for a statement that the model is accurate enough for government use
options.D: Verify which Claude deployment path holds the required FedRAMP authorisation level for this data as of the decision date, and move the production design onto that path

questions.explanation: Government compliance regimes such as FedRAMP apply to the specific service and deployment used.
